t: I might think it is optional; therefore Scripture says "you shall surely lend him". The wording "if" in the commandments of the Torah generally means that if such and such happens, the Torah commands such and such, and accordingly one could understand from the verse that there is no command to lend, but that if a person decides to lend to a poor person, the Torah commands him not to act toward him as a creditor (as stated in the continuation of the verse). But from the verse "you shall surely lend him" we learn that there is a command to lend.
and this commandment is greater than charity to a poor person who asks. Than giving charity to a poor person who asks for charity (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 10:7).
this trait. Of asking for charity.

and the Torah was strict with one who refrains from lending to the poor. Even if he refrained from lending out of concern that the borrower would delay repayment and his debt would be released in the Sabbatical year (see also Hilchot Shemitah 9:4).
one who presses the poor. Pushes him to repay the debt.
and he knows that he has nothing with which to repay him. That he has nothing to repay with, neither money nor the equivalent of money.

transgresses a negative commandment, as it is stated, "you shall not be to him as a creditor". When he knows he has nothing to repay with, the demand pains the borrower for nothing, and the Torah forbids the lender to press the borrower with cruelty that does not help collect the debt (Yad Pashut).

and it is a positive commandment to press the foreigner. Regarding an Israelite, who is "your brother", the Torah commands conduct in financial dealings of kindness and mercy, whereas regarding the rest of the world the Torah commands conduct in financial dealings according to strict law, as customary in the world in monetary matters (see also below 5:1).
it is forbidden for a person to appear before his debtor etc.. As part of the prohibition "you shall not be to him as a creditor".
to appear. To show himself deliberately to the borrower even if he is not claiming from him.
lest he frighten him or humiliate him. For when the borrower sees the lender passing before him, he may become afraid or ashamed of him.
to suppress. To cover, to conceal.
and say to him, "go and come back," when he has it. To put off the borrower, when he has something with which to pay now.

do not say to your neighbor, "go and come back". The continuation of the verse: "and tomorrow I will give (I will repay the debt), when you have (the money to pay now)" (and see below 2:4, that when he is able to pay and refuses to do so, he transgresses a prohibition).
when he claims etc.. See below chapter 22, where the order of collecting a debt is detailed.
that are found for him. That he has in his possession.

and if the movables do not suffice, they collect from the land. Repayment of the debt. must be made with money or with movables that can be sold anywhere for money, so a person who has movables cannot pay with land. But if the court sees that the known movables are not enough, they collect from the land.

after placing a ban on whoever has movables etc.. By enactment of the Geonim, in certain cases when a person suspects another of making a false claim against him and cannot obligate him to take an oath, he may place a ban (a curse) in general terms on whoever lies against him in that matter, without mentioning the suspect's name, in order to threaten him not to claim against him improperly (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:4 in the Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot Gezelah 4:7-8, Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 3:11). And here the Geonim enacted that before collecting from land, the court places a ban (a curse) on one who owes the claimant money and has movables, or on any other person who knows of movables of the debtor and does not bring them to the court.

even though it is mortgaged to his wife's ketubah or to an earlier creditor. To whom he became obligated before he borrowed from this one, and who have priority in collection (as below 20:1), but who have not yet claimed payment from him.

we collect for this one, and if the first comes and seizes, he seizes. We give the land to the creditor who is claiming now, even though it is possible that afterward the earlier creditor will also claim and take the land out of his hands.
a creditor does not etc.. Compare Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 3:14.
that he dyed for them... that he bought for them. That he dyed them or bought them for his wife and sons.
and needless to say if they had rings and ornaments of gold or silver. Jewelry of gold or silver, which are needed even less than Sabbath and festival clothes.

all Israel are commanded to redeem him. For redeeming captives is a great commandment and takes precedence over giving charity to the poor (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:10), and the borrower cannot place this obligation on the lender alone.
they arrange. When collecting from the debtor's property, certain things are left for his use and not everything is taken from him.
the way they arrange in valuations. See Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 3:14-20.
and they give him from everything food for thirty days etc.. From everything he brought, they leave him objects worth food for thirty days, etc.
and clothing. Garments.
and bedding. Sheets and blankets.
and if he was poor. Who is accustomed to simpler conditions.
and a mat. A mat of coarse fabric.
even though he is obligated for their sustenance. For repayment of the debt precedes his obligation toward them, as below halakhah 8.
and his tefillin. His tefillin.
a craftsman. A carpenter, a woodworker.
adzes. Tools for smoothing and leveling wood (Commentary on the Mishnah, Arachin 6:2).
saws. Saws.
and we do not buy him tools with the money of the excess. We do not sell the extra tools and buy a tool of the other type so that he will have two of it.
a donkey driver. One who drives donkeys.
his yoke. The yoke of oxen with which he plows.
these are not vessels. Although he uses them for his livelihood, they are not considered vessels.

and the woman seized movables from the husband's property in order to be sustained from them. For it is the husband's duty to sustain his wife. And when he is absent, she has the option to sell from his property and buy food with it (see Hilchot Ishut 12:16).
for even if her husband were present. Before us.
as we have explained. Above 1:7.
go and seize them. In order to collect the debt from them.
he claimed that he has movables etc.. The lender claims that the borrower has movables that he is hiding in his house.

for the Torah was strict about this, as it is stated, "you shall stand outside". This verse was stated regarding taking a pledge from a borrower (as below 3:4), but the prohibition applies also to entering a house to collect movables for repayment of the debt (see Yad Pashut).
but they place a ban on whoever has and does not give to his creditor. As above 1:4.
because swindlers have multiplied. Who borrow money and afterward claim deceitfully that they have nothing to repay with.
and the door was locked before borrowers. An expression meaning that because of the swindlers, lenders refrained from lending for fear that they would be unable to collect the debt.
a severe oath, like that of the Torah, while holding an object. That he swears while holding a Torah scroll (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8, and see ibid. halakhot 11-12).
and he includes in this oath etc.. He will add to his oath a commitment to repay in the future if he has the means to repay.

but he sets aside from all that his hand attains etc.. Each time he takes from what comes into his hand an amount sufficient for thirty days' food and twelve months' clothing, so that the rest of the sum will be available for collection.
the governors and the prefects. Leaders of the people.
he gives to his creditor, first first. He gives to the earlier creditor and afterward to the later one, as below 20:1.

and they first place a ban on whoever knows of open assets of so-and-so etc.. Before they have the borrower swear that he has nothing with which to repay the debt, they place a ban on anyone who knows that the borrower has movables and does not inform the court, as above 1:4.
for they did not enact to uproot a matter of the Torah itself. The command "you shall stand outside".
money was seen with him. They testified that they saw money in his possession.
or "it is a business in my hand". I received it in order to do business on behalf of its owner.
we do not listen to him. As above 1:4, and he is not believed in his claim even though he swore that he has nothing.
until he brings proof. That it belongs to others.

for one oath covers all creditors, and it is an enactment of the later authorities, and we are not exacting in it to be strict but to be lenient. Regarding his swearing that he has nothing at all, this oath is effective toward all the creditors (see Bavli, Ketubot 94a); and regarding his swearing that all he earns he will give to his creditors, although one might say that he must swear this to each creditor separately, since this is an oath enacted by the Geonim that is not from the law of the Gemara, they were lenient with him that he may swear to all of them together (Lechem Mishneh and Maggid Mishneh).
he nullified a negative commandment of the Torah. Since there is no need for an oath, it turns out that he pressed him to repay when he had nothing to repay with.
and to drive him off. To get rid of him.
and it is stated "until your brother inquires of it". Regarding returning a lost item, that a lost item is not given to a swindler even if he gives signs of it (see Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 13:3).
and he is estimated to have money. By reasonable estimate, he has money.
to make him. To compel him.

for repaying a creditor is a commandment. A person who firmly holds a loan he received from his fellow and refuses to return it transgresses the prohibition "you shall not oppress" (Hilchot Gezelah 1:4), and he has the commandment to return what he oppressed (Responsa of the Radbaz 2:616), and the court has authority to compel observance of commandments.
the gist of the matter etc..
. See Hilchot Sanhedrin 24:1-3.
and his intent is only to pursue justice, which we were commanded to pursue. As stated: "Justice, justice shall you pursue" (Deuteronomy 16:20).
to pervert the law. To act not according to the law.
and admitted to others regarding other debts. He acknowledged to other claimants that he borrowed from them without a document.
and his hand attained more than is proper for him. More than he needs for food and clothing. And by his oath, whatever he earns beyond these expenses he must give to his creditors (above halakhah 2).
only the holders of documents take the excess. Even if according to him the loan without a document preceded the loan with a document, and if so it should have priority in collection.
lest he made a collusion by admitting regarding the property of this one. Out of concern that he devised a ruse and admitted to others deceitfully in order to avoid paying the holder of the document.
they extract from Levi and give to Shimon. Since Levi is obligated to Reuven and Reuven is obligated to Shimon, Shimon can collect his debt directly from Levi.
if Reuven has no property. With which to repay his debt to Shimon.
and he had a promissory note against Levi. A document that Levi owes him money, and Shimon wants to collect the money from Levi for the debt Reuven owes him.
it is a document of trust. There was no actual loan, but the one who signed as borrower trusted the lender and gave him the document, so that he could borrow from him if he needed in the future.
rather Shimon swears. That he was not repaid by Reuven.

like the law of any collector, who collects only through an oath. Anyone who collects a debt from property that is in the hands of a third party and is mortgaged to the lender must first swear that the debt still exists (see below 22:10). And even if the borrower admits that the debt still exists, this is not enough, lest the lender and the borrower be colluding against the property of the third person (Rav Hai Gaon, Sefer HaMikach VeHaMimkar, gate 27).
and admitted to another of his own accord regarding another debt. For which there is no document.
he lent him against a pledge. He lent in exchange for a pledge to secure repayment.
more praiseworthy. Than a loan with witnesses or against a pledge.
and anyone who lends without witnesses transgresses "and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block". For a stumbling block may result, lest the person be tempted and not want to repay.
and brings a curse upon himself. For he will appear to be claiming from his fellow for nothing, and people will say that he made a false accusation against another.

for whatever a slave acquires, his master acquires. Anything acquired by a slave is acquired by his master, so when the master borrows from the slave, the slave gave the master the master's own money.
and all the money in a woman's hand is presumed to be her husband's. All money found in a woman's hand is presumed to be from the husband's property.
from her dowry. The property the woman brought at the time of the marriage (see Hilchot Ishut 16:1).

we do not take a pledge from her, neither at the time of the loan nor not at the time of the loan. We do not take a pledge from her of any kind. There are two kinds of pledge: a pledge the borrower gives at the time of the loan to give the lender security, and a pledge the lender takes when the repayment date comes and the borrower has no money to pay, at which time he takes movables from him to spur him to obtain money and for other reasons mentioned below in halakhah 3 (and he does not collect his debt from these movables because they are things that must remain for the borrower's sustenance as above 1:7, or because the lender is not interested in them but in the money - Yad Pashut).

and not by order of the court. A court agent has authority to take a pledge even in certain cases where the lender has no authority to do so (see below halakhah 4), but regarding a widow even a court agent has no authority to take a pledge from her.

if the pledge was lost or stolen or burned before he returned it, he is flogged. The prohibition is to take the pledge from the widow and keep it with him, so if he returned it as it was and did not keep it, he is not flogged. But when it was lost, stolen or burned and he can no longer return it, he has transgressed the prohibition and is flogged (Yad Pashut; some explain that when he returns the pledge he is not flogged because it is a negative commandment that is cured by a positive commandment, "you shall surely return" - Maggid Mishneh and Derishah 97:15, and see below halakhah 4).
for he lent him against the pledge. That he gave him a pledge in advance at the time of the loan.
with his own hand or by order of the court. Whether he took the pledge himself or through the court.
he shall not take in pledge. He shall not seize as a pledge.
the millstones. For grinding.
and wooden kneading bowls. Bowls used for kneading dough.
and pots. Pots.
as it is stated, "for he takes a life in pledge". "No man shall take the mill or the upper millstone in pledge, for he takes a life in pledge."
and if the pledge was lost or burned before he returned it, he is flogged. As above halakhah 1.
liable. To flogging.
the mill. The lower stone of the mill.
and the upper millstone. The upper stone of the mill.
specified as two vessels. Two separate vessels.

and likewise if he took in pledge a team of oxen plowing, he is flogged twice. If he took from a widow a pair of animals plowing together, he is flogged for each animal (but from another person it is permitted to take plowing oxen in pledge even though he needs them for his livelihood, as below halakhah 5 regarding a plow, for only things used for preparing the food itself are considered vessels of food preparation, as above halakhah 2 - Yad Pashut).

one who lends to his fellow. And after the repayment date has arrived and his fellow has no money to repay, he wants to take a pledge from him (and from here until the end of the chapter the discussion is of a pledge that is not at the time of the loan but at the time of repayment).
he may take a pledge from him only through the court. By order of the court, and if he did not do so he has the law of a robber (Hilchot Gezelah 3:16).
and even a court agent. Who comes with their authority.
he may wrest the pledge from the borrower's hand by force. He has permission to seize the pledge by force.

he is not flogged, for it was cured by a positive commandment etc.. When he returns the pledge he is not flogged for the negative commandment "you shall not take in pledge," because it is cured by the positive commandment "you shall surely return"; but when the pledge was lost and cannot be returned, he is flogged for the negative commandment (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).

whether he takes his fellow's pledge through the court etc.. In any case of taking a pledge, even of things permitted to take in pledge, there is an obligation to return them to the borrower when he needs them.

he returns the pillow at night... and the plow by day... as it is stated, "you shall surely return to him the pledge". Although the verse speaks directly of the duty to return night clothing to the poor, from it we learn the general principle that there is a positive commandment to return the pledge to the poor person when he needs it (see the next paragraph).
"you shall not sleep with his pledge" - this is night clothing. The verse refers directly to night clothing, since Scripture gave the example of sleeping at night.

"you shall return it to him by sunset" - this teaches that he returns it all day. This verse speaks of clothes or vessels used by day, and comes to teach us that they must be returned to the borrower so that he has them all day until sunset ("by sunset"), and then they may be taken from him again (Bavli, Bava Metzia 114b and Rashi there). From this we learn that the negative commandment "you shall not sleep with his pledge" and the positive commandment "you shall surely return to him the pledge" are general commands to the lender to leave the pledge with the borrower when he needs it - day vessels by day and night vessels by night (based on Yad Pashut, and see below the paragraph beginning "you have learned").
so that the debt will not be released in the Sabbatical year. For a debt on which there is a pledge is not canceled in the Sabbatical year (see Hilchot Shemitah 9:14).

and it will not become movables in the hands of his sons. For orphans are not obligated to repay their father's debt from movables they inherited from him (below 11:8). But if he took movables as a pledge, he can collect his debt from them even if the borrower died (and even if the borrower died while the pledge was with him, the lender may take it from the orphans, as below halakhah 6).

transgresses three names etc.. Three separate prohibitions. When he holds the pledge by force at a time when he is not permitted to hold it, he transgresses the warning "you shall not enter his house," which means taking the pledge by force and holding it (even if he did not enter his house), and he also transgresses "you shall surely return" and "you shall not sleep with his pledge," which applies to both day and night clothing as explained in the previous paragraphs (see Yad Pashut).

but if he took it in pledge at the time of his loan, he does not return it at all etc.. For the commands detailed in halakhot 4-5 refer only to a pledge at the time of repayment and not to a pledge at the time of the loan.
things that a person cannot give as a pledge. Which serve the most basic needs (compare above 1:7).
and he returns to him day vessels by day and night vessels by night. As above halakhah 5.

if he had two vessels before him, he takes one and returns one. If he took from the borrower two night vessels of equal use, he takes one outright and returns the other at night, since the borrower does not need both. The same applies if he took two day vessels of equal use (Rashba, Bava Metzia 113a).
that he does not need, and we do not leave them for the borrower. As part of the arrangement at the time of collection (above 1:7).

he leaves them with him for up to thirty days, and after thirty days he sells the pledge through the court. When he took the movables as a pledge it is like a new loan against this pledge, and an unspecified loan is for thirty days, as below 13:5 (see Ra'avad's critique and Maggid Mishneh; but when the movables were taken in order to repay the debt, they do not wait thirty days for the borrower, as below 22:1).
if the borrower died, he does not return to his sons. Things he was obligated to return to their father by day or night.
if the borrower died after the pledge was returned to him. After he returned to him the day vessels or night vessels.
the lender snatches it from his sons and does not return it. He takes the vessel from them, as it does not have the law of the orphans' movables (as above halakhah 5).
the guarantor etc.. One who guaranteed his fellow's loan has a different law than the borrower.

take his garment, for he has become surety for a stranger. From one who guaranteed his fellow's debt, his garment may be taken, and the restrictions on taking a pledge from the borrower do not apply to him.
and likewise one who has wages owed by his fellow. He owes him money but not as a loan.
whether wages for his work. That he worked for a person as a hired worker and demands payment for his work.
whether rent for his animal and vessels or rent for his house. That he rented them to another person and demands the rental fee.
and if he converted the wages into a loan. If they agreed to define the payment as a loan.
"when you lend your neighbor any loan". From this, in any loan ("any loan") it is forbidden to enter and take a pledge even if it was not originally a loan.
its rental is more than its depreciation. That one receives for renting it more than it depreciates through use.

since this is like returning a lost item. When he rents out the pledge, the poor person gains that the debt is reduced through the rental, and if he does not do so the poor person loses the income he could have earned from renting the pledge.
and he does not need the owners' permission. For presumably the borrower agrees to this.
and why did Scripture divide them?. If it is the same prohibition, why is it mentioned twice?

to transgress it with two negative commandments. To reinforce the warning against lending with interest (but these are not two separate negative commandments - see Sefer HaMitzvot, ninth principle and negative commandment 235).
from tradition. The Sages' tradition in explaining the verses.
to be involved between borrower and lender in interest. To take part in carrying out the loan.
a scribe. Who writes the promissory note.
you shall not be to him as a creditor. This prohibition includes every act that creditors usually do, including demanding interest on the loan (Maggid Mishneh).
"do not take from him interest" and "you shall not put interest upon him". The Torah repeated the prohibition of interest in various places to reinforce the warning (see above halakhah 1).
"and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block". A general prohibition on one who strengthens the hands of transgressors and causes them to stumble (Hilchot Rotzeach 12:14).

a guarantor, witnesses and the like transgress only "you shall not put interest upon him". The guarantor and witnesses, and anyone who takes part in the loan transaction, such as the scribe, transgress "you shall not put interest upon him," because they perform an act that sustains the loan that carries interest, and they are like those putting interest on the borrower. This refers to participants who do their part after the loan has already been decided on and would have been carried out without them, so they do not transgress "before the blind" (but a guarantor or witnesses without whom he would not have lent also transgress "before the blind" - Tosafot, Bava Metzia 75b, s.v. arev).
a broker. An intermediary.
instructed him. Commanded one of them to take part in the loan.
because it can be repaid. Returned and the situation restored to what it was; and where there is an obligation of both flogging and payment, if he paid he is released from flogging.
fixed interest. Interest that the lender and borrower agreed upon from the time of the loan (for examples see below 6:1, and see also ibid. halakhah 3).
it is recovered through the judges. The court extracts it from him as one extracts a robbery from a robber.
and if the lender died, we do not extract from the sons. From what they inherited.
their father left them interest money. If he died and left his sons money that he collected as interest.
they are not obligated to return it. The obligation of return is only on the father.
a specific item. Defined and distinguishable.
they are obligated to return it out of respect for their father. For every time others see the item they will remember that the father took it from them improperly.
where he repented and did not manage to return it before he died. Since he repented, they are obligated in his honor.
robbers who returned. Who wished to repent and came of their own accord to return (see Hilchot Gezelah 1:13).

we do not accept from them, in order to open a path of repentance for them etc.. If they are required to pay everything they took, perhaps they will refrain from repenting; but if the item still exists they must return it, and we do not fear that they will refrain from repentance because of this.

and it is itself. He comes to return what he took (some explain that this excludes a case such as where he robbed or took as interest a beam and built it into a building, in which case he need not demolish the building and return the beam, as explained in Hilchot Gezelah 1:5 - Chiddushei Mayim Chaim, Yad Pashut).
their words. Interest that is forbidden by rabbinic law.
the principal. The basic sum against what he lent.
got ahead and collected. In violation of the prohibition.
they extract from him the fixed interest. As above halakhah 3.
the dust of interest, which is rabbinic. Things forbidden by rabbinic law so that people will not come to Torah-prohibited interest (below 6:1).

it is not collected from the borrower for the lender, and it is not returned from the lender to the borrower. The lender cannot collect it from the borrower. And if he collected it, the court does not extract it and return it to the borrower.

it is like one who writes and has witnesses testify against himself that he denied the Lord God of Israel. The very document of interest he made, contrary to what is stated in the Torah, is a denial of God.
and likewise any borrower and lender with interest between themselves. Even if the loan is done privately, it involves denial.
even though he is not particular. That they pay him.
and it is a gift that he gives them. And he does not intend to collect the loan.
and he gave him. Of his own accord at the time of repayment.
severity. The strictness.
more. More than the sum that was supposed to come to him.
in an amount over which the mind inclines. In an amount over which a person might err in counting.
he must return. For presumably he erred in counting and added to him.
he had a robbery in his hand etc.. He slipped into the loan money some money that he had robbed from him (see Hilchot Gezelah 1:8).
by one or two. If he added one or two coins, it is possible he counted them one by one or two by two and erred in the count.
or by five or ten, lest he counted by fives or by tens. It is possible he counted them in groups of five or ten, and erred in the number of groups.

and likewise if he found extra equal to the number of fives or the number of tens, he must return. If the amount added equals the number of groups in the total sum, he must return it, for it is possible he counted the groups using single coins, and afterward mixed them by mistake with the rest of the coins (for example, he borrowed 120 coins and found 132, for perhaps he counted 12 groups of 10, and for each group put aside a coin as a marker, and afterward mixed these 12 coins together with the 120 coins of the loan).
one who lends his fellow on the coin. If it was agreed that he would repay him in a coin of a certain type (see Hilchot Ishut 16:6).
and specified its weight. Stated the weight of the coin in which he would repay.
and they increased its weight. The authorities decreed that the weight of metal in that coin would be greater, but the name of the coin remained as it was.
if produce became cheaper because of the addition. If the purchasing power of the coin increased because of the added weight.
he deducts the amount of the addition for him. So that it will not be like interest.
from the coin current at that time. The heavier coin, in which trade is now conducted, since in practice it is the same coin that was agreed upon.

and they reduced it. They reduced its weight; if they reduced less than a fifth of its weight, he repays him with the new coin. And although in this case there is no concern of interest, they equated the law also in the case of reduction so that the lender will not suffer a loss (Rosh, Bava Kamma 9:12).
and it was invalidated. By the authorities.
to circulate it in another country. To trade with it elsewhere, where the coin is still in use.
and he has a route to that country. He intends to go there anyway.
for they made a kinyan from him. They performed a kinyan sudar on this (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
is of no effect. To permit him to take interest or to exempt him from returning the interest he took.
or gave a gift. He defined the interest as a gift.
for all interest in the world is a waiver. Since the borrower gives it willingly.

it seems to me that this ruling is not correct etc.. A waiver regarding the past is effective (but a waiver of interest he will give in the future is not effective - Maggid Mishneh, which resolves the Ra'avad's critique).
and the Sages said explicitly. See above halakhah 5.
it is permitted to give them to a trustworthy person. On condition that he work with them and they divide the profit.
who has good property. Choice land, whose financial situation is stable and investment with him carries no great risk (see Hilchot Nachalot 11:1).
close to profit and far from loss. In a way that there is a high likelihood that the orphans will profit and not lose.
and if there is a loss there, you will bear the loss alone. And you will pay it to them from your own pocket.
for this is like the dust of interest. Below 5:8.
and regarding the property of orphans they did not decree. For the benefit of the orphans.

and a resident alien. A gentile who accepted upon himself to keep the commandments commanded to the children of Noah because of God's command (Hilchot Melachim 8:11, and see also Hilchot Issurei Biah 14:7-8).

to your brother it is forbidden and to the rest of the world it is permitted. The prohibition of interest is unlike robbery, which is forbidden even against a gentile (see Hilchot Gezelah 1:2), for it derives from the demand on every Israelite to treat his fellow Israelite as a brother from whom it is not fitting to collect interest.
and it is a positive commandment to lend to the gentile with interest. Not only is it permitted, but there is a commandment to lend to a gentile with interest (compare above 1:2).
the Sages forbade etc.. The Sages limited the possibility of lending to a gentile with interest.
except for his livelihood. For the Israelite's subsistence needs and not in order to get rich.
for he flees from him and is not familiar with him. The borrower keeps away from him and is not in regular contact with him.
the dust of interest. Interest by rabbinic law (for its definition see below 6:1).
is permitted to everyone. To every person, and not only to Torah scholars.
give them to me. The loan money, from the gentile.
and I will pay you back as you pay the gentile. I will return the money to you with the addition of interest payments as you would have paid the gentile.
this is fixed interest. For he borrows money from an Israelite and pays him interest.

even if he stood him before the gentile. Even if they agreed in the gentile's presence that the first Israelite would transfer the money to the second Israelite and he would repay the gentile the money and interest, this is forbidden, because in practice there is a loan from Israelite to Israelite (and although the transfer of the money was done with the gentile's consent, we do not say that the second Israelite is the gentile's agent and the loan is as if returned to the gentile and given by him to the second Israelite, for there is no law of agency between an Israelite and a gentile - Bavli, Bava Metzia 71b).
until the gentile takes his money and gives it to the other Israelite. For then an actual loan is made between the gentile and the second Israelite.
"give them to me and I will pay you as you pay an Israelite" - this is permitted. Since there is a loan made between the gentile and the second Israelite, unrelated to the first Israelite.

and if he stood him before an Israelite. If they agreed in the Israelite's presence that the gentile would transfer the money to the second Israelite, and he would pay the first Israelite the money and the interest.

even though the gentile gave the money into his hand, since he gave it with the Israelite's knowledge, it is fixed interest. Although the act done here is the gentile's giving into the second Israelite's hand, nevertheless since the Israelite lender is present at the giving and agrees to it, the gentile's giving is considered merely a technical act done because of the first Israelite's wish, and as if he himself gave to the second Israelite (based on Yad Pashut, and see Maggid Mishneh, Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh, who found this halakhah difficult).
to place his money in the hand of a gentile etc.. To give it to a gentile so that he will lend for him to another Israelite with interest.

for since their law is that the guarantor is claimed from first etc.. According to gentile law the lender collects his debt from the guarantor, and the guarantor then collects from the borrower (unlike Jewish law, in which the borrower is claimed from first, and only if he has nothing do they collect from the guarantor, as below 25:3). So the guarantor is like an intermediary in the loan, as if he borrowed from the gentile with interest and then lent to the borrowing Israelite with interest, and when the guarantor collects the money from the borrower he turns out to take interest from him.

therefore if the gentile accepted upon himself not to claim from the guarantor first, this is permitted. For if the borrower is claimed first and has nothing to pay and the guarantor pays in his place, the entire payment (the principal and the interest the guarantor paid the gentile) is regarded as a new loan that the guarantor lends the borrower, and when it is returned to the guarantor there is no interest here (see Rashi and Ramban, Bava Metzia 71b).
and he charged them to him as a loan. He added the interest to the loan itself and the debt was defined in advance by the whole sum.
if before he converted he charged them to him as a loan, he collects the principal and the interest. For at the time he converted everything was defined as debt and not as interest.

and if after he converted he charged them as a loan, he collects the principal and does not collect the interest. For he is forbidden to collect the interest after he converted, although the loan was given when he was a gentile.
lest they say, "this man converted on account of his money". That he converted in order not to pay interest.
all interest money for which he became obligated when he was a gentile. But what he became obligated for after he converted is forbidden as interest.
and one who gives his money close to loss and far from profit. The giver bears the loss payments, and the profits are divided between them.

and it is forbidden for a person to give his money etc.. It is forbidden to give a person money to work with if the recipient will bear all losses and they divide the profits (see above 4:14 and below 8:12), for if the recipient must in any case return the sum he received, the money he received is in fact a loan, and the profits are interest.

they divide the profit and the loss according to the law of the business. The giver also bears the losses in accordance with his share in the profit as is customary in a business (see Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin chapter 6).
we do not set up a shopkeeper for half the profit. A person may not give another produce and the like to sell for him in return for dividing the profit equally.
and he may not give him money to buy produce for half the profit. That he buy produce and sell it, and they divide the profit equally.
and we do not appraise calves and foals to fatten them for half the profit. It is forbidden to give one's fellow animals to fatten on condition that they divide the profit equally.

unless he gives him payment for his labor and his food. He gives him payment for his effort and for the expenses of feeding the animals. The problem in all these cases is that if the recipient in the end returns the principal and they divide the profit, then the work was done in return for receiving the thing as a loan, and this is forbidden as interest. But if he receives payment for his effort, then he worked for his wage and not in return for the loan.
or that the profit of the worker exceed his share of the loss. That he participates in the losses in a reduced proportion, which is his payment for his effort.
as we explained regarding partnership. Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 8:1.

one who goes into partnership with his fellow... he may not combine the profit with the principal etc.. When he invests with his fellow in a partnership or business, and gives him the money and they write a document about it, he may not estimate the profit in advance and write it as part of the principal, lest there be no profit or less profit than expected, and when he collects according to the document his fellow turns out to pay him interest.

and likewise he may not give him money as a business or partnership and write it as a loan etc.. Even if they write only the principal, they may not define it as a loan, lest there be a loss and he die, and the heir not know of it and collect the whole principal without deducting his share of the loss.
it is forbidden to advance etc.. Even an addition that was not agreed on is forbidden, even if it was given outside the time of the loan.
he set his eyes on borrowing from him. He planned to ask him for a loan.
gifts. Gifts.
on account of his money that was idle with him. That he could not profit from it while it was in the borrower's hand, and it was idle with the borrower.
and needless to say he may not praise him in words or rise early to his door. All the more so he may not praise him or arrive early at his house to greet him.
as it is stated, "interest on anything". For even non-monetary benefits are forbidden as interest.

he may not say to him, "let me know if so-and-so came from such-and-such a place" etc.. Even when the benefit does not come to the lender directly but to another person whose welfare the lender is interested in, it is forbidden as interest.

there are things that are like interest and are permitted. That look like interest because the giver receives more than the sum he gave, but are permitted because the additional payment is not payment for the extension of time of the loan, and there is no interest here at all.

a person may take his fellow's documents and his fellow's debts for less, and not be concerned. It is permitted to buy from one's fellow the right to collect a debt, by document or orally, for less than the amount of the debt, for the reduction is due to the risk that he may not succeed in collecting the debt. And although in exchange for what he gave the seller he will receive the right to collect more than that, this is not considered interest.
and a person may give his fellow a dinar so that he will lend so-and-so a hundred dinars. So the lender receives from the two of them together more than he lends.
for he gave him only payment for speaking. The payment is for the mediation between the parties, and there is no additional payment for the loan itself.
there are things that are permitted. And in the loan itself there is no interest or dust of interest.
and it is forbidden to do them because of the concealment of interest. The Sages forbade them because indirectly there is an addition for the loan.
I have wheat worth a maneh. Wheat worth a hundred dinars that I can sell you on credit, and you can sell it and receive the money you need.

and he went back and bought it from him for ninety. The seller himself went back and bought from his fellow the wheat he had sold him, and paid him in cash a sum lower than the sum for which he originally sold it to him.
this is permitted. Since the additional payment is not because he sold to him on credit, but from the fact that there were two sales with a price difference between them.
but they forbade it because of the concealment of interest, for he gave him ninety and takes a hundred. And the purchase was only a way to circumvent the laws of interest.
and if he transgressed and did so, he collects the hundred from him. The hundred that he owes him for the wheat he originally sold him.
for there is not even the dust of interest here. Therefore the law here is not like the dust of interest, which is not collected from the borrower for the lender (above 4:6).

and likewise one who had his fellow's field mortgaged in his hand etc.. That he received from the borrower his field as a pledge for a loan (for the various ways in which this is permitted or forbidden see below 6:7-8).

he may not go back and rent it to the owner of the field. If the borrower himself rents the pledged field from the lender, it is forbidden as concealment of interest, for the field truly belongs to him, and it turns out that the rental payment is a way to circumvent and pay the lender interest for the loan.
it is forbidden to rent out the dinars. To give them for a period for payment, and he may return other dinars.
and brings other dinars. And it resembles a loan.

and this is the dust of interest. But it is not fixed interest, since it is not like a loan because not all responsibility is on the renter (for a renter is exempt for circumstances beyond control), whereas in a loan he must return the entire sum in every case (see Tosafot, Bava Metzia 69b).

a king whose laws were etc.. If according to the king's laws one who paid a tax imposed on his fellow can in return enslave his fellow to work for him (see also Hilchot Gezelah 5:16, Hilchot Avadim 1:8).
and paid a dinar on his behalf. Paid a tax worth a dinar for him.
even though he is enslaved to him for more than a dinar, this is permitted. And there is no interest in this, since the payment he made for his fellow is not considered a loan.
a sela for five dinars. He lent him a sela (worth four dinars) on condition that he repay him five dinars.
or a sela for a sela and a se'ah. He lent him a coin of a sela on condition that he repay him a sela and a se'ah of wheat.
any loan with any addition is interest of the Torah. Also called "fixed interest" (above 4:3). All this provided that the addition was fixed and defined in advance (see below halakhot 2-3).
and stipulated with him that he live in his courtyard free until he returns his loan. And the dwelling is in addition to repayment of the loan.
or rented from him for less etc.. The lender agreed with the borrower that he would rent his courtyard for a certain sum, less than the usual rent, until he repays the original debt.

a place where its produce is plentiful at the time of the loan. Where the profits from the property are certain and carry no risk, in which case they are treated as a fixed payment (and if the profit is not guaranteed it is not interest by Torah law, as below halakhah 7 regarding a field).

for example, he pledged his courtyard on condition that he live in it free. The borrower gave the lender his courtyard as a pledge for the loan, and they agreed that the lender could live in the courtyard without paying rent, and this is a certain profit from the property.
this is interest of the Torah and is recovered through the judges. As above 4:3.

and likewise one who sells a field or courtyard with asmakhta etc.. Asmakhta is a commitment dependent on a future condition, which has no acquisition force because the transferor thinks the condition will not be met and does not make up his mind to transfer (see Hilchot Mechirah 11:2-6 ff.). And since the sale does not take effect at all, the money the buyer paid is a loan, and the produce he ate is interest.
and the same applies to anyone who did not make a complete acquisition at first. Even if he stipulated that the acquisition would be completed later, as below halakhah 6.

because if he ate the produce, it is interest of the Torah. Since the sale did not take effect, the money was given as a loan to the seller, and in return for this loan the lender was given permission to eat from the produce (and although Torah interest is only when it is agreed in advance, as explained below halakhah 2, here they agreed in advance that he would take his field and eat its produce, so it is considered Torah interest - Even HaAzel).
and this is called the dust of interest and is not recovered through the judges. See also above 4:6.
he may not draw his slave. He may not take the borrower's slave to himself.

even though the slave sits idle. He does not do work for his master, and he does not lose anything from the lender taking him to work for him, and nevertheless this is forbidden as the dust of interest.
even though the courtyard is not made for rent and its owner is not accustomed to rent it out. That the courtyard is not intended for rent and the householder does not usually rent out his property.
and if he lived there, he must pay him rent. To avoid the dust of interest.
this is the dust of interest. And not fixed interest, which is forbidden by the Torah.
because he did not stipulate with him that he lend him and live in his courtyard. For they did not agree on this payment in advance.

and he came to collect the rent of the courtyard in which he lived against the debt. The borrower wants to deduct and offset against the debt what would have been proper to pay him as rent of the courtyard.
if the rent was equal to the debt, he does not deduct all of it. They do not fully offset the amount of the loan so that the borrower would not have to pay the lender anything.
rather as the judges see fit. They set a certain sum to deduct as a compromise between them, and the borrower pays the rest (based on Mirkevet HaMishneh).

for if you remove him with nothing, it is as if he extracted it through the judges etc.. Removing the lender from the property without any payment is like collecting the interest money from the lender (and see also below 7:1).
as it is stated, "you shall not give him on interest". This implies that the Torah's prohibition applies only if the initial giving was with interest, and not if it was agreed on afterward.

one who lends his fellow against a field etc.. He pledged the field as security for repayment of the debt, and stipulated with him that if he does not repay the loan by a certain time, the field would be acquired by the lender.
he has not acquired. Even though the borrower agreed to the condition and the condition was met.
because it is asmakhta. As explained above halakhah 1.
therefore he deducts all the produce he ate etc.. He deducts them from the sum of the debt, for since he did not acquire the field, the produce he ate is fixed interest (ibid.).

if I do not return to you within three years, acquire it from now. They agreed that if he does not repay the loan within three years the field would be acquired retroactively from now, and in this way it is not considered asmakhta (see Hilchot Mechirah 11:7).
and he brought him within three, he has no produce. Since there is no sale, and eating the produce is in return for the loan.

if he did not bring it within three, all the produce belongs to the buyer. The lender acquires the land retroactively from the time of the loan, and it turns out that he ate produce from his own field (and until the matter is clarified, the produce is held by a third party, as explained below halakhah 6).
he did not acquire. By the law of asmakhta.
and all the produce he ate is fixed interest. As above halakhah 4.
but if the buyer said to him with his knowledge etc.. Then the sale takes effect, but the buyer takes upon himself to return the land to him without cancelling the sale.
acquire in proportion to your money. He transferred to him from now a part of the land corresponding to the part he paid.

when you bring the rest of the money you will acquire from now. That he will acquire the whole field retroactively, from the time of the first acquisition. But if he does not bring it, he will not acquire at all, and the seller will return to you the money he gave him.
lest the buyer bring the rest of the money and the field turn out to be his. Already from now, and if the seller eats produce, it is interest on the remainder of the debt.
and likewise the buyer is forbidden, lest he not bring. And the sale will not take effect, and if the buyer eats produce it is interest on what he gave the seller, which turns out to be a loan.
a third party. A third person who serves as a trustee over the produce.
when you bring the rest of the money you will acquire. That he will acquire the whole field only at the time of delivery of the full payment, and does not acquire anything from now.
the seller eats the produce until the buyer brings. Since the field is his until the buyer pays him.
"acquire from now, and the rest of the money is a debt with you," the buyer eats the produce. For the field is his from the time of the first payment.

and if the seller ate, they extract from him everything he ate. For he eats interest for the delay of payment, and this is fixed interest (as above halakhah 1 regarding one who eats produce from a field that is not his at all).

and he pledged his field to him on condition that he eat all its produce all the days of the pledge. The borrower gave the lender his field as a pledge so that he could eat its produce throughout the loan period (for a fixed time or until repayment, see below 7:1).
even though he does not deduct anything for him. That the lender does not deduct from the debt the produce he eats from the field.
this is the dust of interest and is not recovered through the judges. For although they agreed on it in advance, it is not fixed interest but only the dust of interest.

for one who pledges a field is not like one who pledges his courtyard. Whose law was explained above halakhah 1, that if he pledged his courtyard on condition that the lender live in it free during the loan period, the profit is certain and is considered fixed interest.

for there is no certain produce in the field at the time of the loan etc.. As long as there is no certainty of profit but a loss may instead occur, the interest he receives by eating the produce is not considered fixed.
to one who sold with asmakhta. That the produce he ate in this case is considered fixed interest even in a field, as above halakhah 1.

for one who sells with asmakhta did not make up his mind and transfer it. The land, for asmakhta does not acquire, and in practice there was no sale at all but only a loan of money. For this reason the interest is given to the buyer at the time of taking the produce from the field, and because the profit is at that point certain and he does this with the seller's agreement from the start, it is fixed interest (Chiddushei HaGra'ch, Even HaAzel, and see Yad Pashut).

and the one who pledges did make up his mind and transfer this body for its produce. In the pledge discussed here the borrower transferred to the lender the body of the land, so the fact that the field's produce is not guaranteed means that the giving of the land is not a complete giving of interest.
and this appears from the Talmud etc.. From the Talmudic discussion (Bava Metzia 62a), it emerges that eating the produce of a pledge without deduction is the dust of interest.

and you must establish it only as one who pledges his field. For from another place it appears that they ruled that a pledge without deduction is fixed interest recoverable through the judges (see ibid. 67a), and the passages cannot be reconciled unless one distinguishes between the pledge of a field and the pledge of a courtyard (see Maggid Mishneh, and see below halakhah 8).
he pledged to him a place whose produce is constantly found... this is fixed interest. As explained above halakhah 1.
he pledged to him a field and the like... this is the dust of interest. As explained at the beginning of the halakhah.
and likewise if he pledged a courtyard and the like with deduction etc.. As explained in the next paragraph.

"I deduct for you a ma'ah of silver each year as rent for this land, so that all its produce will be mine". He subtracts from the debt a fixed sum for each year, defined as rent for the land, even though the sum is small.

in a courtyard and the like it is forbidden. Although he deducts for him a certain sum as rent for the land, since the profit is certain he is considered as renting from him for a reduced sum because of the loan (based on Rashi, Bava Metzia 64b, quoted in Lechem Mishneh).
and in a field and the like it is permitted. Since he may lose and receive nothing in return for the deduction, he is considered only as buying something with a certain risk (ibid.).

and they did not descend to the depth of the matter to distinguish between a field and a courtyard. They were not careful to distinguish between the cases, as Maimonides distinguished above halakhah 7.
and so they ruled that every pledge, even with deduction, is forbidden etc.. As the dust of interest.

how so? etc.. In the following cases are explained forms of pledge that are permitted even according to the Geonim who forbade the pledge with deduction (and according to Maimonides these cases are permitted even in a house and courtyard, in which a pledge with deduction is forbidden).

and stipulated with him that after ten years this land will return to its owners free. They stipulated that use of the land during the stated period would be in return for the entire sum of the loan, and at the end of the period the borrower would not need to pay the lender anything more, and his land would return to him.

even if its rent was worth a thousand dinars each year etc.. Although the rent for this land is much higher than the sum of the loan, it is permitted because the loan itself is regarded as a cheap rental payment for the field and not as a loan, since no money is returned at all at the end of the period.

and likewise if the owner of the field stipulated with him that whenever he brings him money he will calculate ten for each year and remove him from it. The method mentioned in the previous paragraph is permitted even if the borrower stipulates that he can take the field back in the middle of the years of the pledge, if he calculates the portion repaid from the loan according to the years and pays the rest of the debt. The commentators explained that the difference between a pledge with this calculation and the pledge with deduction mentioned above at the end of halakhah 7 (which is forbidden in a courtyard according to Maimonides, and according to the Geonim even in a field) is that here only the property is pledged for payment of the debt and there is no additional obligation on the borrower. For the lender cannot return the land in the middle of the years of the pledge and demand the remainder of the debt back, and in addition even if the field is damaged and yields no produce at all, the lender cannot collect his debt from other property of the borrower. For this reason the transaction is defined as a cheap rental of the field and not as a loan. By contrast, in a pledge with deduction the debt is not paid only from the property itself but remains on the borrower, so it cannot always be seen as rental (Maggid Mishneh).

and likewise if the borrower stipulated that whenever he wishes he will calculate for him what he lived etc.. Also in a house or courtyard given as a pledge, the borrower may stipulate as with a field that whenever he wishes they will calculate the years that have passed and proportionally reduce the debt, and he will pay the rest and take the property back.
and every condition in a rental stands, as we have explained. Hilchot Sechirut 7:1.

and he pledged his field to him until a fixed time or until he brings him money and he removes him, and the lender ate all its produce. Without deduction or another agreement, and this is forbidden as the dust of interest, as above 6:7.
we do not remove him with nothing. Rather only part of the debt is deducted, as above 6:2.
and needless to say if he ate more than his money, we do not extract from him. It is clear that the lender is not required to return to the borrower what he ate beyond the sum of the debt.

and likewise we do not calculate from document to document in a pledge. If he borrowed with two separate documents and pledged to the lender two fields for the two loans, we do not count what he ate beyond the debt from one field as part of the repayment of the debt in the second document, but each loan is judged on its own.
if the land pledged was in the hand of orphans etc.. We look to the benefit of the orphans, and we are strict with the lender to fully offset the loan against what he ate.
he ate more than his debt, we do not extract the excess from him. For we are not strict with him to the point of extracting money from him.
a place where they were accustomed to remove the lender whenever he brings him money. That the borrower may repay the lender his debt and take back the pledged land whenever he wishes.
that the lender may not be removed until the end of the pledge period. Until the time set in advance, even if the borrower repays him the debt before then.
and anyone who pledges without specification. Without setting a time for the pledge.

and the lender stipulated with him that he not be removed... he cannot remove him. Since the borrower delivered the land on this condition, it is clear that he agreed to this and no kinyan is needed for it.

and the lender accepted upon himself to be removed... he must acquire from him on this. To do a kinyan sudar on his commitment to withdraw (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there), so it will be clear that the lender's waiver of his right was made seriously (Yad Pashut).

a pledge in a place where the custom is to remove the lender whenever he brings him his money etc.. A pledge from which the lender can be removed at any time is not considered acquired by the lender during that time, and this has several implications detailed here.

a creditor of the lender does not collect from it as he collects from land. One who collects from an heir can collect only from the land that belonged to the lender and not from other property (below 11:7). And in the case of a pledge from which one removes the lender, if the lender died and the pledged land came to his heir, the lender's creditor does not collect from it, since this land is not considered land belonging to the lender.

and the firstborn does not take a double portion in it. For the law of the firstborn is to receive a double portion in property that was in his father's possession at the time of his death (see Hilchot Nachalot 3:1-5). And a pledge from which one removes the lender is not considered something held in the lender's hand.

and the Sabbatical year cancels it. The Sabbatical year cancels the debt of loans, but a loan on which there is a pledge is not canceled (above 3:5, and see Hilchot Shemitah VeYovel chapter 9). A pledge from which one can remove the lender is not considered acquired by the lender, so it does not have the law of a pledge that prevents cancellation of the loan.

and when he removes him, he does not take even fruits that ripened and fell to the ground. Rather the lender leaves them for the borrower who removes him, since the land in which the produce grew does not belong to him.
and a place where he cannot remove him etc.. If he cannot be removed, the lender's right of possession in the land for that period makes it considered his, and the law changes in those cases.
even though this pledge is forbidden and the dust of interest, as we have explained. Above 6:7, so the question arises why the Sages dealt with it and detailed its laws.

it is possible that this custom is in error or among gentiles etc.. It is necessary to detail the matter so that in places where they are accustomed to pledge, by mistake or deliberately, they will know the status of the lands. It is also needed for cases of lending to gentiles, for it is permitted for anyone to lend to them with the dust of interest (above 5:2).

since it is the dust of interest, we follow the custom. Because this is a rabbinic prohibition and not Torah, weight is given to what was customary in the various places (to remove or not to remove), and we do not say that it is a custom without halakhic force.

and there is one who ruled that this pledge is with deduction. That the laws mentioned above in halakhot 2-4 speak of a pledge with deduction, which is permitted ab initio in a field (as above 6:7), and so it is understood why they detailed its laws.
a gentile who pledged his courtyard to an Israelite. And during this time the Israelite lives in his courtyard and does not pay him.

the pledger need not pay rent etc.. Although the Israelite who took the pledge continues to live in the courtyard until the gentile repays his debt, he need not pay the Israelite who bought the courtyard rent, since he took the pledge from the gentile, and according to gentile law the pledge is fully acquired by the lender until repayment.

and the owner of the land was the one eating its produce. And there is no prohibition in eating the produce since the owner eats it, but the lender added a condition to the pledge that if the pledged land is sold in the future, only he will have the right to buy it.

"you may sell it only to me for this price" - this is forbidden. Since he fixes the price in advance, it appears as if he reduces the price for him in return for the loan (Maggid Mishneh). Some explained that it is possible that when he wishes to sell the field's price will be higher, and it turns out that he lowered the price for him in return for the loan (Sefer HaNer in the name of Rabbeinu Baruch).
and if he said to him, "sell it to me at its worth" etc.. According to the land's value at the time of sale, and there is no reduction because of the loan.

it is permitted to increase the rent of lands etc.. In renting lands there is no concern of interest when he charges more money if the renter pays each month than he would charge if he paid the whole sum at the start. For since the time for payment of rent is only at the end of the rental period, the proper sum is what he will pay at the end of each month, and it is possible to give a discount if he pays everything in advance, and there is no prohibition of interest in this (Bavli, Bava Metzia 65a).

and he said to him, "give me two hundred zuz with which I will improve the field" etc.. The renter asked the field's owner to lend him two hundred zuz so he could spend on the field's needs, and said he would pay higher rent each year.

this is permitted, because if he improves the field with these dinars its rent will be higher. Since he gave him money that he can invest in improving the field, the field is more profitable, and the addition of two kor is for the rental and not for the loan.
and I will dig it out. I will make improvements and excavations to beautify it.
this is permitted. Here too the additional payment is for the rental of a better shop or ship.
and I will raise the rent for you. I will add to you in rent.
this is forbidden. Since the shop or ship itself was not improved, it turns out that he added to the rent for the loan.
that is worth silver. One silver coin.

and it is permitted for a person to say to his fellow etc.. It is permitted to repay work with work if it is the same work and in equal conditions, but not if the conditions differ, for then there is concern that he will repay with harder and more expensive work for postponing repayment.
all the days of the dry season are one. All the days of summer are considered equal, and it is permitted to repay work with work of the same type in them.
and all the days of the rainy season are one. All the days of winter are considered equal.
for the toil of plowing in the rainy days is greater. Because the ground is wet and the days are short (based on Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 5:10).
one who hires a worker in the days of winter to work with him in the days of cold. He pays the worker in the winter days for work he will do with him later when the cold days arrive.

because he appears to lend him today so as to reduce his wage. For he paid him in advance, and the work that is worth more than the payment he will do with him later, and this resembles repaying a loan with interest.
but if he said to him, "work with me from today until such-and-such a time for a dinar each day". That he hired him from that day onward.

he does not appear as taking payment for his money that he advanced and gave him for his wage. The reduction of the wage is not like a loan of the money in advance, for he begins to work now, but is like immediate payment for the work, in which there is no problem of interest.

it is forbidden to increase on a sale. Although it is permitted to increase on a rental (above 7:8), they did not permit increasing on a sale, since in a sale the duty to pay is at the time of the purchase.

this is the dust of interest. Interest by way of sale was not forbidden by the Torah, so even if they agreed in advance on the addition for late payment, it is not considered fixed interest but is forbidden as the dust of interest (Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 173).

for this resembles one who takes twenty because he gave him a hundred to use until such-and-such a time. When the seller demands an addition for postponing the payment date, it appears as if the seller lent the buyer the hundred he committed to pay for the purchase and collected an addition of twenty in return.

and when he claims him in court, he is obligated to give him only what it was worth at the time of the sale. For the addition is the dust of interest, which is not collected from the borrower for the lender (above 4:6).

or he returns his sale to him if it still exists. The seller may cancel the sale and demand that the buyer return the goods he bought if they still exist in his hand. For the seller can claim that he sold on the understanding that he would receive a high price at the agreed time, and since it turned out that he cannot receive this price, he wants to cancel the transaction (Lechem Mishneh).

and likewise if he sold him movables etc.. Where the movables have a known price, it is forbidden even if he stated only the price if the buyer pays later. But for land, which has no fixed price (and likewise where the movables had no fixed price), there is no prohibition unless he also stated the price if the buyer pays immediately at the time of purchase.
he may say to him, "give me immediately for less". Since he is not raising the price for the delay in payment but, on the contrary, reducing it if he pays now.

a barrel of wine worth a dinar now, and he sold it to him for two until the summer. And in the summer it will be worth two and then the buyer will sell it, so the seller adds to its present price because of waiting for payment until summer.
on condition that if a mishap occurs to it, it is in the seller's responsibility until the buyer sells it. The seller bears the losses from damage that may occur to the barrel until it is sold.
this is permitted, for if it is lost or broken he pays nothing. And such a transaction is not at all like a loan, in which the seller has no responsibility.

and if he did not find a way to sell it and profit on it, he had to return it to its owner. The commentators found this sentence difficult, since the condition that he return it to the owner if he does not sell it is mentioned here only in the case in the following paragraph. Some hold that inability to sell is also included in the mishap in the condition (see Yad Pashut, and likewise Beit Yosef, Perishah and Bach on Yoreh De'ah 173, who discussed on this basis the relationship between what is written here and the case mentioned in the next paragraph; and see Shakh, who wrote that this sentence is the reason for the law in the later paragraph and should appear there).
whatever exceeds two will be your payment for your trouble in selling it. If you sell the barrel, the entire sum above two will be yours, as payment for your effort.
and if you do not find a way to sell it as you wish, return it to me - this is permitted. For this is not a complete sale, since the buyer can return the barrel if he does not sell it as he wishes.
even though if it is lost or stolen or turns sour it is in the buyer's responsibility. For the seller is not responsible for a defect in the barrel itself or the wine.
if he had produce etc.. If at the seller's home produce sells for more than in the market.

he may sell them for twelve until twelve months. He may sell to him for twelve and the buyer will pay him after twelve months, for the seller is not adding for the delay of payment, but this is the price he would have demanded even if the buyer had paid him now.

it is forbidden to buy the fruit of an orchard before it is complete and ripe etc.. When the buyer pays in advance, before the fruit ripens, and pays a cheap price on that account, the discount is like payment the seller gives for the time the money is in his hands until the fruit ripens.

and death is a common thing. And since there is a reasonable possibility that the buyer will lose during the waiting period, the reduction in price for early payment is balanced by the risk that he will lose his money (compare above 5:8).
one who gives money to the owner of a vineyard for the branches and the vine cuttings. In order to take the vine branches after they are cut.
and they buy them cheaply until they dry and are cut. He pays in advance at a cheaper price.

he must turn them while they are attached etc.. To hoe under the vines. By this he is considered to have now acquired the body of the vine for the sake of its cuttings, and the money is not considered a loan for a future purchase. Some explain that he turns the branches or cuttings while still attached to the tree, and thereby acquires a right in the body of the vine (Yad Pashut).
and if he did not turn them, the money turns out to be a loan... and it is forbidden. As explained in the previous halakhah.

field guards etc.. Field guards whose work ends when the work in the field is finished but who receive their wages in wheat only after the work on the threshing floor is finished, and because of the postponement of payment the wheat is calculated for them at a price lower than its value - this is the dust of interest, and to avoid this they must help with the work on the threshing floor so that their work continues until the time of payment, and thus the additional wage is not for the postponement of payment.
they remove them from the field in Nisan. When the grain is harvested, and the sharecropper pays his share.
and the sharecroppers give them four se'ah for every kor of seed. The sharecropper pays the owners four se'ah of grain for every kor.
and this one left his sharecroppers in his field until Iyar and took from them six se'ah. He gave the sharecropper additional time to work in the field, and collected from him a higher payment.

this is permitted and there is no name of interest here. Since the additional payment is not for the postponement of payment, but so that the sharecropper can finish working the field and make additional profit from it.
and likewise the price. That is the fixed price in the market at that time.
for there was no stipulation there. That he pay in advance in order that he give him more, but rather he added of his own accord.

it is permitted for a person to give the price of a barrel of wine to his fellow etc.. The buyer pays in advance for a barrel of wine he will receive at a later time, and stipulates that the seller will be responsible if the wine turns sour, and he accepts that he will receive according to the agreed price even if the price changes.

for since he accepted the cheaper price, he is close to profit and to loss. There is no prohibition in this, for there is a certain risk to the buyer, since the price may fall. But if the buyer did not accept this upon himself, it turns out that the seller accepted all responsibility for the wine in return for early payment, and this is forbidden as the dust of interest (see above 5:8).

and likewise it is permitted for a person to buy from his fellow in Tishrei a hundred jars of wine for a dinar and not take them until Tevet etc.. Here too he pays in advance for wine he will receive later, but here it is not a case of buying a particular barrel (as in the previous paragraph) but of a general commitment by the seller to supply a hundred jars of wine. And although the seller accepts responsibility for the wine turning sour, this is not considered interest for advancing the payment, since it is defined that he bought from the outset only the jars that contain wine and not vinegar, and clarifying which jars he bought is done in Tevet when he takes them.

to rent the ship and take its rent etc.. To rent out a ship for rental payment, in addition to the renter's responsibility to pay for the loss that occurs to it. This may appear to be interest, since the renter must fully repay the value of the ship as it was at the time of renting (like a loan), and in addition pays rent (which is like interest).

this is permitted. It is not a loan, for the body of the ship belongs to the lessor (for if the price of the ship changes, the renter does not pay the difference), but a rental with greater responsibility on the renter (and this is permitted, as explained in Hilchot Sechirut 2:9).

and he received them from him to tend them etc.. He received the flock to tend, and in return he receives a certain percentage of the offspring, the wool and the milk, and in addition he accepted responsibility to pay the value of the flock if they die.

this is forbidden, for the owner of the flock is close to profit and far from loss. For the owner of the flock takes part in the profit but bears no responsibility for the flock (and see above 5:8-9).

one who appraises a cow from his fellow etc.. One who rents an animal and stipulates that if it dies he will pay for it according to its present value, in addition to the rental payment. This may appear to be interest, since the renter must fully repay the value of the cow agreed between them (like a loan), and in addition pays rent (which is like interest).

permitted, since he made it a fixed value only after death. It is not a loan but a rental, since he did not accept responsibility for its price while alive (for a decline in its value) but only payment after its death, so the cow belongs to the lessor throughout the rental (Rashi, Bava Metzia 69b).

and a woman rents to her friend a hen to sit on the eggs for two chicks a year. She rents her friend the hen to brood on the eggs, and in the end the renter returns the hen itself and payment of two chicks from those that hatched from the eggs.
and there is no concern of interest here. For this is a rental and not a loan, as above halakhah 13.

when they extract from him, they extract five from him, since it came to his hand as interest. Although he added to him of his own accord and it was not part of the interest they agreed on, this is not judged as a mere gift, but since he gave him this addition as part of the fixed interest, all of it is interest.

and likewise if he gave him a garment or a vessel with it etc.. If the borrower gave utensils as payment for the interest he owes the lender, the item itself is extracted from the lender's hand, and he may not return its value to the borrower. The reason is so that people will not say that he uses vessels of interest (Bavli, Bava Metzia 65a).
he rented him with them etc.. If they agreed that he would rent him a place whose rent is three dinars, in return for the four that he owes him as interest.

when they extract from him, they extract four from him etc.. Although in practice he profited only three from this, they extract four from him, since by agreeing to rent that place for four dinars he regarded it as worth that, and lost to himself.
we do not fix a price on produce. To set in advance a price that the buyer pays now for certain goods, and the seller will supply them later.

until the price comes out. Until a stable price has been set for the produce (see below halakhah 4). For otherwise it might turn out that he sold at a price lower than what will be set, and it is as if there had been a loan with interest.

even though this one has none, that one has. Even if this seller has no produce, he may fix a price, since the produce is available in the market and the buyer can obtain it now at this price, and it turns out that he did not profit from waiting for the money.
in what case is this said?. That it is forbidden to fix a price before the price is set.
if the seller had any of that kind. Even if he has a little and the buyer fixes with him for a large quantity (Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 175, unlike the understanding of the Maggid Mishneh).
even though its work was not yet completed. That not all the preparation of the goods before their sale was complete.
first to the harvesters. He harvested the grain early and the price was not yet set.
for they are still in a heap. They are still lying in a pile in the field.
in the vat. A pit in which grapes are gathered.
in the olive-press yard. The place where olives are gathered until they soften.
once he sinks it in the kiln. Once he has placed the stones in the kiln to burn them to produce lime.
once the potter makes their eggs. Once the potter prepares from the clay round balls in the shape of eggs, from which clay vessels are shaped.
when their earth is white. It is high-quality clay from which fine clay vessels are made, and it is not found everywhere.
but black earth. Ordinary clay.
even though they were not yet made. He had not yet prepared the eggs.
lacking one more labor. Until it reaches the state in which it is customarily sold.
to roll by measure. Rolling to a measure.
provided that it is the buyer's way to take them out of the kiln. For then placing them in the kiln is the final labor.
"what my goats milk is sold to you" etc.. He sold him the future produce in advance.
