this is permitted. Since the price does not depend on the quantity there will be, and it is not clear whether he profits or loses from it.
but if he said to him, "such and such what my goats milk is sold to you for such and such". That he bought for a certain sum a certain quantity of produce.

it is forbidden unless he fixed with him according to the market price. For when the produce does not exist in the seller's possession we do not fix a price on produce, unless we fix it at the market price (above halakhah 1).
we do not fix on the price of towns etc.. If a price has come out in a particular town, it cannot be agreed that he will supply produce at that price, for the price in towns is not stable and fixed.
the province. The central city or region within whose bounds the town lies.

if the wheat was etc.. If it was the custom that the price of old wheat is a quarter higher than new, we do not rely on this until the price for both kinds has been explicitly set (Yad Pashut based on the Rif).
gleaned wheat. Wheat gathered from various fields, whose quality is not excellent.
and he may not fix for the householder until the price is set for the householder. One cannot fix on the householder's wheat on the basis of the price of gleaned wheat, until it is explicitly set.

once the price is set, he may fix on the high rate. He may set a price on the basis of the present price, and stipulate that if at the time he supplies the goods the price falls, he will buy at the cheaper price (the "high rate" is the cheap price at which more produce can be had for the money).
he gives him according to the price at which they were worth when he gave him the money. Since he did not explicitly stipulate that he would give him at the cheap price.

and one who retracts receives the curse "mi shepara". The sale can be canceled since the completion of acquisition is at the time of giving the produce, but he must accept upon himself "mi shepara," the Sages' curse on one who does not stand by his word (see Hilchot Mechirah 7:1-2).
whether the seller or the buyer. Whether he is an agent of the seller or of the buyer.
for the sender says to him etc.. For certainly the sender intended that he would stipulate with him to supply at the high rate.
and the sender does not receive "mi shepara" on account of the agent. The sender is not obligated to accept "mi shepara".

for the sender says to him, "I sent you to repair, not to distort". The agency is on the understanding that the agent benefit the sender and not spoil and harm him, and since the agent did not carry out his agency properly (for an ordinary person's intention is toward the high rate), the sender may retract from the agent's act and does not receive "mi shepara" for it.
as we have explained. Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 1:2.

and took the money on condition that he give him five for a sela etc.. The seller received the money in advance on condition that he supply the buyer later wheat at a price lower than the market rate.
if he has wheat, it is permitted. For he is like one selling cheaply, since he could give him the wheat now.
he had wheat owed to him by others etc.. He committed to supply wheat for less than the market rate, on the basis of wheat owed to him.
for they still lack collection. They must be collected from the borrower, and are not in the seller's possession.

and it is like one who fixes a time and reduces for him because he surrounds him. It appears that the reduction in the price of the wheat is a payment the seller gives for the time the money is in his hands until he supplies the goods to the buyer.

it is permitted to give a sela to the merchant so that he brings him six se'ah from the village. Although he supplies the merchant at a price lower than the market rate, this is not seen as an addition in repayment for the advance payment to the merchant, but rather as the merchant buying for him in a place where the price is cheap.
provided that they are in the buyer's responsibility etc.. The responsibility is a sign that the purchase was made in the villages for him.
and a prominent person is forbidden to do this. Because of the appearance of interest.

and in types of merchandise it is forbidden to everyone, because types of merchandise are not always found like produce. For it is possible that the merchant will not find that same merchandise to buy cheaply, and will repay him with something whose price is higher than what was agreed.
to their brokers. Merchants who buy goods from them and sell them to others.
with money that they gave them at first when they entered the city etc.. As repayment of money lent to them when they entered the city, before they began to sell.
their sacks. Their sacks.

for these do not sell to them cheaply because they gave the money now and will not take until after a time etc.. The reduction is not an additional payment for the loan they lent them (for if so it would be forbidden as interest), but is because these acquaintances or brokers will help them by telling them the price in that place, or will assist them in other ways in their trade (Meiri, Bava Metzia 73a).
one who carries produce from place to place. From a cheap place to an expensive place.
"and I will give you produce that I have in that place". I will give you in return the produce there, which in practice is more expensive.
if he has some there, it is permitted. For this should be seen as an exchange and not a future repayment in return for an addition.
from place to place. From a cheap place to an expensive place.

"give it to me and I will pay you its price as it is worth in that place". The buyer will take the goods to that place and sell them, and after a time pay the seller their value in the expensive place.

if it was in the seller's responsibility until it reaches there, it is permitted. If the goods remain in the seller's possession and responsibility until they reach the expensive place, he sold them to the buyer only when they arrived there, and there is no interest problem in returning to him the expensive value.

and if it was in the buyer's responsibility, it is forbidden. Since the responsibility is on the buyer, it is as if he borrowed the goods from him in the cheap place, and the later payment at the expensive rate is forbidden as interest.
the price of ten of these cucumbers, the price of ten of these melons etc.. That he bought from him those particular gourds while they were still small.

and stipulated with him that he give them to him when they grow large, this is permitted. Although the price is cheap relative to large gourds, this is not considered an additional payment for advancing the money, because in practice he bought them while small.
for he leaves them and they grow on their own. By themselves, with no need for the seller's involvement.
and if he had cut them now while small, others would not have come in their place. Therefore the seller suffers no loss in that the buyer did not take them from the field at the time of purchase.
and likewise anything similar, of a thing in which there is no loss or deficiency to the seller. For if there is a deficiency or loss, it is seen as interest for advancing the payment.
just as it is permitted for the seller etc.. As explained above 9:1.

so it is permitted to borrow produce without specification and repay it without specification, without setting a time, at the market price. Like the seller, who may fix a price on produce after the price has been set, it is also permitted to borrow produce after the price has been set. But unlike a sale, a loan of produce for produce is permitted only if no specific time for repayment was set.
even though the wheat became expensive. And according to its monetary value, it turns out he returned more than he borrowed.
for if he wished he could buy and return to him, since he did not set a time. Since he could repay him immediately another se'ah at the same cost, there is no interest in this.

and if it became expensive, he takes the money for which they were worth at the time of the loan. And it is forbidden to return produce in the measure he gave him, because of interest, since the produce is now worth more than it was worth at the time of the loan.

if he had some of the kind he borrowed etc.. Another possibility of permission in a loan of produce for produce is when the borrower already has produce of the same kind, in which case it is permitted even if the price has not come out, provided he did not set a time for him.
jars of wine and oil. Barrels of wine or oil.
or they did not know the market price. The lender and the borrower, even though the price has come out.
until he turns them into money. He lends him on condition that he repay him money according to their present value.
he should not say etc.. Because he set a time for repayment.
to the threshing floor. The end of the harvest.
but he says to him etc.. Since this is not considered setting a time.
borrowed produce until a fixed time. And this loan is forbidden.
if they became cheaper, he returns produce to him at the time he fixed. Although the loan was in violation, because he is not adding to him.
he gives him the money for which they were worth at the time of the loan. So that he will not transgress the prohibition of interest by giving him produce that is worth more.

a person may lend his sharecroppers wheat for wheat for seed. A person is permitted to lend wheat for sowing to the sharecroppers who work his field for a proportionate share of the grain, and they will repay him after the harvest. And although in this manner he sets a time for repayment, it is permitted.

in what case is this said? etc.. The permission to lend wheat for wheat for seed is only in the case that at the time of the loan the landowner could remove the sharecropper from the field and dismiss him, for the reason that will be explained in the next paragraph.

in a place where the custom is that the sharecropper provides the seed etc.. If the custom in that place is that the sharecropper supplies the seed, and as long as he has not brought seed the landowner can remove him.
if the sharecropper had not yet gone down. Only if he had not gone down to the field and begun working it.

it turns out that when he goes down to the field he goes down on the understanding that he will return the wheat he lent him. Since the loan was made before the sharecropper took the field into his hands as a sharecropper (as long as the owners could remove him), it turns out that when he goes down to the field and commits to give the owners their share of the crop, he includes in it the wheat he must return to them, and its return does not look like repayment of a loan but like the owners' share of the grain that grew.
for seed. On condition that he sow them and repay him after the harvest, in which there is the setting of a time for repayment.
without specification. Without setting a time for repayment.
"go and make them upon me at the present price etc.". Calculate the amount of wheat that can be bought with the sum of the debt, and I will be obligated to repay you such an amount of wheat.
if he has wheat to the amount of his money. If the debtor has wheat in an amount equal in value to the money he owes his fellow.

for the Sages did not say that it is permitted to fix on the market price etc.. Although it is permitted to fix a price on produce if the price has come out or if he has a little of that merchandise (above 9:1), in this case, where supplying produce is a substitute for repaying a loan, one cannot rely on the price having been set, but he must have wheat and in sufficient quantity to repay the entire debt.
if the borrower had wheat etc.. Even if he converts the supply of wheat into supply of wine, it still has the law of a debt, and there is no permission unless he has wine.

if he did not have etc.. If he had no produce and nevertheless converted the monetary debt in violation into a debt of produce, he is not obligated to repay in produce even if he has produce later (for although they agreed between them he may retract and there is no "mi shepara" in this, since the fixing was done in violation of interest - Or Sameach).
or he said to the witnesses, "be witnesses against me" etc.. And when he admits in this manner this is testimony that obligates him to pay (see Hilchot Edut 17:4).
therefore if he later claimed and said, "I paid". And the lender claims that he did not pay him.
he swears a lesser oath. An oath enacted by the Sages for a defendant who denies the entire claim against him (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:3).

he must pay him before witnesses. So that they will testify that the document is paid (but if the lender returns the document to the borrower or writes him a receipt of payment of the document, witnesses are not needed).
he is not believed. To claim "I paid" if the lender claims he did not pay him (although the Sages enacted that the borrower can require the lender to swear that he was not paid, as below 14:2).
therefore one who says to the witnesses etc.. Because of the difference between an oral loan and a loan by document, care must be taken not to write a document on an oral loan.
they turn. They turn.
to consult him. To ask his consent.
they made a kinyan from him that he owes him. They performed a kinyan sudar to strengthen the matter (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
they write and give. They write a document about the debt and give it to the creditor, and from then on this debt is considered a loan by document.
for an unspecified kinyan stands for writing. When they made a kinyan on the debt, they intended that a document would be written on it even if this was not said explicitly.
and they do not need to consult him. Regarding writing and giving.
and had witnesses sign it. Had witnesses sign it.

even if there are no witnesses on it, and he gave it to the lender before witnesses, this is a loan by document. Although witnesses did not sign the document, the witnesses of its delivery make it a loan by document (for a similar law in a get see Hilchot Gerushin 1:15).
that it be a writing that cannot be forged, and the witnesses read it. So that it cannot be forged and the witnesses see what was written, for otherwise the lender could change what is written in it.
and there is one of the Geonim who ruled... sign and testify. So that the document will have publicity (Maggid Mishneh), and this is written in a separate document (Kesef Mishneh).
and there are no witnesses there. Signed on the document.
whose handwriting was established in court. That the court confirmed the document and verified that it is his handwriting.
this is like an oral loan in every respect. Since the loan was not publicized as a loan by document (see below halakhah 4).
not from the heir. For one does not collect from him on an oral loan (except in certain circumstances, as explained below halakhah 6).

and not from the buyers. Who bought land from the borrower. For with a loan by document, the lender may collect his debt from all the property mortgaged to him, even from property the borrower sold, but with an oral loan he cannot collect from property the borrower sold (below halakhah 4).
and he collects from the buyers, as will be explained. Below 18:1.
and an oral loan, he collects it from the heir. On the conditions explained below, halakhah 6.

and he does not collect from the buyers because it has no voice. The loan was made without publicity, and the buyer cannot guard against buying the borrower's mortgaged land, so the Sages enacted that with an oral loan one does not collect from buyers.

and the buyer lost by his own doing, for he did not ask etc.. Since the loan is publicized, the buyer from the borrower could have investigated and known that this land is mortgaged and that the debt might be collected from it.
the borrower's property. The land, but movables are not mortgaged by Torah law (below halakhah 7).
one who sells his field before witnesses and it was taken from the buyer's hand. The field was mortgaged to creditors of the seller and was taken by them.

even though there is no document there etc.. The seller is responsible for the field he sold, and if it is taken from the buyer he must return to him the purchase price (Hilchot Mechirah 19:3). And since the sale was done publicly, even if done without a document, the buyer can collect his debt from mortgaged property that other buyers acquired after he bought the field.
as will be explained. Below 21:1.
except in one of these three things. In which it is evident that he did not pay him.
when the debtor admits etc.. That the father admitted the debt before his death.

or they excommunicated him until he gives, and he died in his excommunication. They excommunicated the father because he did not want to repay the debt, and he died before they lifted the excommunication, and had he paid they would have lifted it from him (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:14).
if witnesses came that their father owed this one a maneh. For example, he admitted before them, not close to his death, that he owed the lender.
or that before us he lent him. The witnesses saw the loan itself.
lest he paid him. The father.
as we have explained. That the borrower's handwriting is treated like an oral loan and need not be paid before witnesses (above halakhah 3).

a borrower who has no movables but has land etc.. Repayment of the debt must be made with money or with movables that can be sold anywhere for money. However, when the borrower has no movables he can pay with land, and need not trouble himself to sell the land and pay the lender with the sale money. And if the court learns that he has money to pay but claims that the money belongs to others, the court penalizes him and forces him to sell from his lands and pay the lender with money.

and if this matter is not known to them, they place a ban etc.. When it is not known to the court whether the borrower has movables, they place a ban on anyone who takes part in hiding the borrower's money, and afterward collect from his land (see above 1:4 and the commentary there).
they go down to the medium of his property. They collect from his medium-quality land (and not from the best or the worst of his).
as will be explained. Below 19:1.
even if they were deposits or loans with others. And are not in the heir's hand.
for movables are not under a creditor's lien by Torah law. And since movables are not mortgaged for the debt, the heir need not repay his father's debt from them.

it is a commandment upon orphans to repay etc.. Although the movables in the orphans' hand are not mortgaged for the debt, nevertheless there is a commandment upon the orphans to repay from the movables, out of respect for their father (Rashi, Ketubot 91b).

and if a creditor seized during his lifetime, he collects from them. If the lender held the movables as a pledge for repayment of the debt while the borrower was alive, they became mortgaged to him and he can repay his debt from them.
the heir must bring proof. The heir must prove that the lender seized only after death, for the lender is now in possession of the movables and the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract.
or the lender swears etc.. If the heir did not bring proof, the lender is made to swear on his claim, and he collects his debt from what he seized.
and he can claim up to their value. The lender can claim that the amount of the debt is up to the value of the item he seized.
documents. Promissory notes that others owed to the deceased.

because he does not claim to acquire their body but for the proof in them. Holding the document itself does not give him ownership of the debt (without another document explicitly stating that the debt was transferred to him - see Hilchot Mechirah 6:10-11), so he cannot claim that they are his (as he can claim with seizure of other things), but only that he held them as a pledge. And because he cannot claim that the documents are his, he is not believed to say that he held them as a pledge during the lifetime (Lechem Mishneh).
orphans who collected land for a debt owed to their father by others. After their father's death the orphans collected land from debtors who owed their father.
a creditor of their father may go back and collect it from them. One who lent to their father by document may collect his debt from this land.
for this land is their father's. And was mortgaged to his debts, although it was not in his possession when he died.
and Shimon charged the price of the field to himself as a loan to Reuven. Shimon did not pay for the land, and it was agreed between them to define the payment as a loan.

and a creditor of Reuven came to seize the field from Shimon. This field was mortgaged for a debt that Reuven owed another person, and after Reuven's death that person came to seize the field from Shimon.
and Shimon appeased him with money and he went away. Instead of giving him the field, Shimon paid him, and that person dropped his claim to the field.

the law is that Reuven's heirs may come and claim from Shimon the loan he charged to himself. Reuven's heirs may demand that Shimon pay them the price of the field sale, which became his debt to their father.

for it is not mortgaged to Reuven's creditor. The debt Shimon owed Reuven is not mortgaged to Reuven's creditor, so when Shimon paid him the debt he was not released from the debt he himself owes Reuven, but must pay it to the heirs.

he gives them the land that he took from Reuven for the loan he charged to himself. Instead of repaying them the debt in money, he returns the land to them (and although generally he cannot pay with land when he has money, here they permitted it so that he not suffer a loss - Maggid Mishneh).

and he goes back and seizes it from them because of the money he gave to Reuven's creditor. After returning the land to them he may collect it from them again, to recover the money he paid to the creditor of their father.

for he took it from Reuven with a guarantee. And since he has a guarantee, Reuven's property is mortgaged for the debt, including land that the orphans collected for a debt others owed their father (as explained above halakhah 9).
the Geonim already enacted etc.. See also Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 8:12.
in the West. Spain or North Africa.

they would write in documents of debt etc.. They collect movables by virtue of the explicit condition in the document and not by virtue of the enactment (for a similar practice in writing the ketubah see Hilchot Ishut 16:7-8).

and it turns out that he collects by this condition more than by the enactment. For in addition to collecting movables by virtue of the enactment, in these places they would also collect by virtue of the explicit condition in the document (Lechem Mishneh in understanding of the Maggid Mishneh; and see Kesef Mishneh in the name of the Rivash, that in collecting by virtue of the condition he may collect his debt from movables even when there is land, which he cannot do in collecting by virtue of the enactment).
and a fence. A safeguard and a correction against possible mishap.

lest the borrower did not know of this enactment etc.. For if a person did not know of the Geonim's enactment and borrowed money on the understanding that it would be collected from him according to Talmudic law, he did not mortgage the movables for repayment of his debt, and it turns out that collection from the orphans is not according to law (Responsa of the Rivash, no. 292).
one does not collect from heirs unless they were adults. For then a loan by document is collected from them.

but from minor heirs one does not collect a promissory note. But in cases where an oral loan is collected from heirs, it is also collected from minor orphans (Maggid Mishneh, Kesef Mishneh; and see below 14:1).
even if it contained every condition in the world. For example, it is written in the document that the lender is believed to say that his debt was not repaid.
lest they have proof by which they would void the document. For example, a receipt stating that part of the debt was paid, and while they are minors they do not know where to look for it.
if the loan was gentile interest. That their father borrowed from a gentile with interest.
for the interest eats into their property. And as a result of delaying payment of the debt, a loss is created from the accumulating interest.

they appoint a guardian for them and the court attends to their property. They appoint someone in charge of their property, who handles payment of the debt from their property. [Note: the vocalization of the word "apitropos" follows the Greek original. In the Commentary on the Mishnah in Maimonides' own hand, several vocalizations of this word appear: sometimes the first peh has a kubutz, sometimes a patach (and in some places the peh is not vocalized).]

a woman who claimed her ketubah. Who demands that the orphans pay the ketubah from their father's property; the ketubah is a financial commitment document that the husband writes to his wife at the time of marriage that she will collect it if he divorces her or she is widowed.
for the woman's charm etc.. So that the woman will have money and will find favor in people's eyes and they will want to marry her.
if the woman jumped ahead and married. She hastened to marry before collecting her ketubah.
we do not attend to her. We do not hear her claim.

for she has no maintenance. For besides the reason of the woman's charm, another factor in permitting collection of a widow's ketubah from the orphans' property is payment of maintenance (Kesef Mishneh). While the woman is a widow, she collects maintenance from the heirs as long as she has not claimed payment of her ketubah (Hilchot Ishut 18:1). Therefore they permitted her to collect her ketubah from the orphans' inherited property so that it would not be consumed by the maintenance she takes. But when the woman becomes betrothed, she stops receiving maintenance and it ceases to be a reason to permit collecting the ketubah from their property.
and she has married. She has already married, and does not need the ketubah money in order to marry.

for if the property was equal to the ketubah only or less than it. The value of the orphans' inherited property is equal to the ketubah or less than it, and after collecting the ketubah from the inherited property nothing of the property would remain for the orphans.
for we do not attend to them. We do not collect the ketubah money from the inherited property while they are minors.

for they did not say we attend to orphans' property to collect the ketubah from it except etc.. According to these Geonim, the reason for permitting collecting the ketubah from the property of minor orphans is only because of the loss in paying maintenance and not because of the woman's charm that they will want to marry her (Maggid Mishneh). Therefore, in a case where the orphans have no loss from paying maintenance (since in any case the widow will collect all the property from the orphans for the ketubah), they did not permit her to collect the ketubah while they are minors, even though she needs the ketubah money in order to marry.
the one who bequeathed them. The one who left them the inheritance.

we attend to them after appointing a guardian for them to argue their claim. They pay according to the command even while they are minors, but appoint a guardian to act for their benefit to leave in their hands the good lands and the like.
and they need not appoint a guardian for them. Since the thing to be given was clearly defined.
who seized his fellow's field with his slaves. Took his slaves and by means of them took the field of his fellow by force.
if he has witnesses. That this field is his.
that it was purchased by him from their predecessor. He bought it from the one who bequeathed it while he was alive.

that he held it and ate its produce for the years of chazakah during their father's lifetime. He used it and benefited from it for three years, so that in this way the field comes into his presumptive ownership and he is believed to claim that he bought it from the previous owners (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 11:2). And now he wants to remove the field from the orphans who hold it.

for we do not accept witnesses not in the presence of the litigant etc.. Removing the field from the heirs' hands is done on the strength of the witnesses of chazakah, and there is no way to accept them while the heirs are minors.

and the minor, as if he were not standing here, is regarded. And even if he is actually present at the trial, accepting testimony in his presence is regarded as accepting testimony not in the presence of the litigant.

he validates the document and they remove etc.. When the claimant comes to remove the field by virtue of a document, he can remove it even while the orphans are minors, since validation of documents is done even not in the presence of the litigant (Hilchot Edut 3:11).
they appraise the land. They estimate the value of the land being put up for sale for repayment.
and they proclaim it for thirty days. They publicize its sale so that a buyer will be found at a high price.
sixty days, Monday and Thursday. They proclaim on Mondays and Thursdays over a period of sixty days.

and they proclaim in the morning and in the evening etc.. On all the days of proclamation they announce the sale of the field when the workers go out to the fields and when they return from the fields, so that anyone interested in the field will remember to take workers there to inspect it for him.
they delineate the field by its boundaries. Like "specify" (and so the reading in some manuscripts), that is, they mark its borders.
how fine it is. How much can be produced from it.
and for how much it is appraised. What its value is according to the appraisal made for it.
because there is one who wants to give to a creditor. Who is willing to accept even damaged coins.
and there is one who wants to pay a woman. Who is willing to receive the money in several payments (Bavli, Arachin 21b).
the adrakhta. A document in which the court strengthens the claimant's power to collect from the defendant's property, whose writing precedes the proclamation and appraisal (see below 22:6-9).

they write in it "and we recognized that these assets are of so-and-so the deceased". For only the property the orphans inherited is mortgaged to their deceased father's debts, and not property that they have of their own.

and they do not eat produce by it, even after the proclamations were completed. For when the process is done properly, the claimant eats the field's produce from the time the days of proclamation are completed (below 22:12), but since the adrakhta was invalidated, a new adrakhta must be written and the proclamations started anew.
like one who erred in a matter of a Mishnah. An error in a clear and known matter, and their sale is void, for a judge who erred in a matter of Mishnah, his ruling is void (Hilchot Sanhedrin 6:1).
and the court that sold the guarantee upon the orphans. If the land is taken from the buyer for a reason connected with them, the orphans will have to pay the buyer.

even though they erred and sold a maneh's worth for two hundred or two hundred for a maneh, their sale stands. Since they sold with proclamation and people assessed the quality of the property and the correctness of the court's appraisal, there is no appraisal in error here and the sale stands (Meiri, Ketubot 99b).
but if they did not examine the appraisal etc.. After they made the proclamation (Kesef Mishneh).

a letter of inspection that is etc.. A document about the proper conduct of the proclamation and appraisal, stating that the court was careful as far as they were able (Commentary on the Mishnah, Ketubot 11:5).

and they erred and exceeded by a sixth or fell short by a sixth, their sale is void. Generally when there is an error of up to a sixth the sale stands and the difference must be returned, and when the error is more than a sixth the sale is void (Hilchot Mechirah 12:2). But when a court errs the law is different, and even with an error of a sixth the sale may be canceled (see ibid. 13:10).
less than a sixth, their sale stands. For with a difference of less than a sixth, it is everyone's way to waive (ibid. 12:3).
if they sold the land at a time when they need not proclaim it. At times when there is need to sell the land quickly and there is no time to delay and proclaim (as explained shortly).
at a time when they sell land for burial. To finance the burial expenses of the deceased or of one of the orphans.
for the maintenance of the woman and the daughters. Who are supported from his property after his death (see Hilchot Ishut 19:11).
the king's portion. A tax paid to the king.
because the matter is urgent. These needs are pressing and the time does not allow waiting.
they will hear. That they are up for sale.
and if the market was near the province, they bring them to the market. For they may be sold for more (see also Hilchot Nachalot 11:2).
that he swear. That the debt was not repaid (see also below 14:1).

and we do not suspect a receipt. There is no concern that the debt was repaid and that instead of returning the promissory note to the borrower the lender gave him a receipt releasing him from the debt.
takes his fellow's money. Which he borrowed from him.
locks the door before borrowers. So that they will refrain from lending to them.
to validate the document in his hand. To authenticate the witnesses' signatures to prevent concern that the document is forged (for the laws of validating documents see Hilchot Edut chapter 6).

the court does not attend to him until the borrower comes and claims. The court does not intervene and prevent him from selling the pledge until a hearing in the borrower's presence, but allows him to sell immediately (Lechem Mishneh; and if the borrower comes and claims that he repaid the debt, the lender will have to swear while holding an object that his debt was not repaid, as explained shortly).
and they give him advice. They advise him.
so that the borrower will know for how much it was sold. And there will be no later dispute over how much money the lender received from the sale of the pledge.

whether the borrower died first or the lender died, since he collects from what is under his hand. Unlike an ordinary debt, which cannot be collected when the borrower dies before the lender (below 17:3), in a loan with a pledge he can collect from the pledge after death since he could have claimed that the pledge is his.

he swears while holding an object and takes. As in other cases of collecting from an heir, who must first swear that the debt was not repaid (below 14:1; and here, since the lender also died, the heir swears that his father did not instruct him that this debt was paid, as below 17:1).
he swears while holding an object. While holding a Torah scroll in his hand (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).
in the manner of all who swear and take. See Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:2.

and why does he not swear a lesser oath?. But a severe oath while holding an object, and he is now in possession of the pledge, and one who is claimed against regarding something in his hand is released by a lesser oath, which is a light oath without holding an object.

because he does not swear about the pledge itself but about the money he takes. For if he claimed that the pledge is his and wished to exempt himself from the owner's claim, he would be released by a lesser oath, like one who denies the entire claim against him. But here he wants to collect his debt from the pledge, so he swears while holding an object like those who swear and take.

but if there were witnesses there etc.. In the previous paragraph it said that the lender swears while holding an object and is not released by a lesser oath, because he did not claim that the pledge is his but that he holds it as a pledge for a loan. Here it explains why he is not released by a lesser oath on the claim of migo ("since he could have said") that the object is his.

if there were witnesses there that this object is a pledge in his hand and they did not know for how much, he can take only by an oath. When there are witnesses who testify that this is a pledge but do not know the amount of the debt, the lender must swear in order to collect from the pledge the sum he claims the borrower owes him.

and since there are no witnesses there... he is believed to say, "I have against it such and such". Since there are no witnesses that the object is pledged in his hand, he is believed to state the amount of the debt, for he has a migo claim that he could have claimed that the object was purchased by him.

and likewise in the oath itself that he would have sworn if there were witnesses that it is a pledge. According to the printed editions and some manuscripts the word "and likewise" does not appear here, and the meaning is that the lender's credibility to claim the amount of the debt is specifically through the same oath he would have had to swear if there were witnesses that it was a pledge. It seems one should explain our reading "and likewise in the oath itself..." similarly, and the meaning is: in addition to his credibility itself by virtue of the migo ("and likewise"), he must also swear the same oath that he would have sworn if there were witnesses (see the note of Rabbi Y. Shilat in the Mugah Rambam).

for we do not say migo to release him from an oath etc.. A migo claim is effective to release the defendant from a monetary obligation, but it does not release him from an oath he is obligated to take (for further examples see Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 9:4, Hilchot Sechirut 2:8). Therefore his credibility to say that it is a pledge does not release him from the oath.

but to release him from payment, that he need not return the pledge until he takes what he claimed. By virtue of the credibility he may continue to hold the pledge as long as he has not received his debt back.
for the lender on a pledge is liable for the value of the pledge. For one who lends against a pledge is considered a paid custodian over the pledge, and is liable for theft and loss.
as we have explained. Hilchot Sechirut 10:1.

"I lent you a sela against it and it was worth two dinars". The loan was for the sum of four dinars (a sela), while the pledge was worth two dinars, and according to his claim a debt of two dinars remains after subtracting the pledge's value from the debt.
and the borrower says, 'You lent me a sela on it, and it was worth a sela'. His claim is that nothing remains of the debt.

the lender first swears the oath of bailees that it is not in his possession. The severe oath taken while holding a sacred object, which the Sages instituted for a bailee who claims that the item was stolen or lost, even when this does not exempt him from payment (see there 6:1).
and the borrower swears a heset oath. Where the lender claims two dinars from him and the borrower denies everything.
the lender says, 'I lent you a sela on it, and it was worth two dinars'. His claim is that a debt of two dinars remains.
and the borrower says, 'You lent me a sela on it, and it was worth three dinars'. So one dinar remains owing, not two.
and afterward the borrower swears... for he has admitted part of the claim. And he is obligated to take a Torah-level oath (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:1-2).

the borrower says, 'You lent me a sela on it, and it was worth two'. He claims that the pledge was worth two selas, and the lender owes him a sela, the difference between the amount of the debt and the value of the pledge that was lost or stolen.
and the lender says, 'I lent you a sela, and it was worth a sela'. His claim is that he owes him nothing.

and he includes in his oath that the pledge was equal to the debt. Together with the bailees' oath that the pledge is not in his possession, he also swears about its value. When a person is obligated to swear on several claims, he is made to take a single oath covering all of them. And if he is obligated to take one light oath and one severe oath, he takes the severe oath and includes all the claims in it (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:14).
the borrower says, 'You lent me a sela on it, and it was worth two'. And he claims that the lender owes him a sela.

and the lender says, 'I lent you a sela, and it was worth five dinars'. The lender admits only that he owes one dinar of the sela that the borrower claims from him, and for this he is liable to the oath of one who admits part of a claim.
I lent you a sela on it, and it was worth two dinars. Therefore a debt of two dinars remains.

for he knows for certain that he owes him and does not know whether he repaid him or not. For the borrower agrees on the amount of the debt, but does not know whether the lost pledge was worth the full amount of the debt or not. And one who is unsure whether he repaid a debt or not must pay (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:9).
You lent me a sela on it, and it was worth two. And he claims that the lender owes him a sela.
I do not know its value. What its value was.
and he is exempt, for he did not obligate himself in anything. The lender is exempt since he did not admit to any sum (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:8).

You have fifty with me, and fifty I do not know. The plaintiff says he lent him one hundred, and the defendant admits to fifty and, regarding the remaining fifty, says he does not know whether he owes it or not.
he is liable to an oath. That he owes him only fifty, like one who admits part of a claim.
and he cannot swear. Since he does not know for certain that he owes him only fifty. And the rule is that one who is liable to a Torah-level oath and cannot swear must pay.
as will be explained. Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 4:7 (and see also Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 5:6).
and he may place a ban. The lender may place a ban on one who makes a false claim against him and causes him to pay unjustly (for the ban see above 1:4 and the commentary there).
even though they did not make a kinyan from him. They did not perform a kinyan sudar (acquisition by handkerchief) confirming that he would not claim him until that time.
whether the borrower died or the lender died. The agreement on the repayment date is not void even though one of the parties is no longer alive.
to claim it on that very day. On the same day that he borrowed from him.
for a monetary condition it is. And they may stipulate as they wish.

like other claims. For the lender demands that the borrower pay now and the borrower denies that he must pay now. The law is that of an ordinary monetary claim: if he denies everything, he swears a heset oath, and if the plaintiff has one witness testifying in his favor, the defendant is liable to a Torah-level oath (the 'oath of one witness' - see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:1-2).

they say to the lender, 'Wait until the end of the five days,' and he swears a heset oath that five days remain. For only then is it a monetary claim that requires an oath, and not merely a dispute over the repayment date, which does not require an oath (since an oath is required only in the case of a monetary claim - ibid. 1:15).
if the loan was by a document and the borrower claimed, 'You fixed a time for me'. And the time has not arrived, and the document does not state a repayment date.

it appears to me, etc.. For in a loan by a document the borrower's property is mortgaged to the lender, and since the document has no date the lender has an immediate right of collection, and the borrower can remove this right from the lender only by bringing clear proof. Therefore the lender may swear a heset oath against the borrower's claim, and collect.
a loan may be claimed in any place, etc.. Unlike a deposit and a lost item, which are claimed only in their place (see Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 7:11).
the borrower came to repay him in the wilderness. And the loan was made in a settled area.
one who impairs his document. The borrower claims that he paid the entire document, and the lender admits that he was paid part of it and holds the document.
and one who comes to collect not in the presence of the borrower. Above 13:1.
and one who seizes from the buyer. See below 22:10.
and one who collects from the heir. If the borrower died and left property, see above 11:6.
collects only with an oath like a Torah-level oath. An oath taken while holding a sacred object, like the law of those who swear and collect (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:2).

and if the debt was for a set time and he claimed at its time, he collects without an oath, etc.. In the cases mentioned here where he collects only with an oath, this refers specifically to when he comes to collect after the repayment date has arrived. Before that he need not swear, since there is a presumption that a person does not repay within the term (above 11:6).
they make him swear while holding a sacred object, etc.. See below 14:12, that the borrower must first bring the money of the debt, and then the lender swears and collects.
or that he paid him only such and such. In the case where the borrower claims that he repaid part of the debt.

and if the lender was a Torah scholar, they do not involve themselves with his oath. The court withdraws from the discussion of his oath and does not obligate him to swear, because it would appear as if they suspect him.
an authenticated document. Whose signatures were examined and confirmed in court.

or he claimed that this debt is interest or the dust of interest. The debt comes from fixed interest, which is forbidden by the Torah, or from the dust of interest, which is forbidden by rabbinic law, and interest is not collected from the borrower whether it is forbidden by the Torah or by rabbinic law (see above 4:6).
an amanah. A document that the borrower gave the lender without having borrowed, and they trusted that he would use it only if he lent him money.
to swear like a Torah-level oath, like one against whom it was claimed that he was repaid. As above, halakhah 2.

for he admitted to the document, and it stands to be repaid. When the borrower admits to the document but claims he paid it, his claim is strong enough to require the lender to swear, since every document ultimately stands to be repaid.

but all these claims are not enough to void an authenticated document. When he makes a claim that comes to void the document, his claim is not accepted at all and he cannot obligate the lender to swear while holding a sacred object before collecting his debt.

rather, he pays, and afterward he may claim against the lender whatever he wishes, etc.. The borrower must pay first, and afterward he can make him swear a heset oath, as can be done in any monetary claim that the defendant denies entirely.
the borrower swears and gives half, for he admitted part of the claim. And even though the witnesses testified that he paid everything, a litigant's own admission is stronger than witnesses.

and it is not like one who returns a lost item, because the fear of the document is upon him. In a case where a person could have denied the lender's claim and nevertheless admitted to part of it, he is like one who returns a lost item to the lender, and the Sages exempted him from swearing, just as they exempted one who returns a lost item from swearing when the loser claims that he returned only half of the lost item (see Hilchot Gezelah va-Avedah 13:20). But when the borrower is afraid to deny the claim for some reason, such as the fear of the document, he is not considered one who returns a lost item; rather he is treated like any other who admits part of a claim and must swear. This is because the reason he does not deny everything is that he is not comfortable lying and brazenly facing his creditor (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 4:5 and the commentary there).
from free property. From the land in the borrower's possession, and not from mortgaged property that was sold to others.
and they have voided this document. And what he collects, half, is by virtue of the borrower's admission, which is treated as an oral loan, which is collected only from unmortgaged property.
for he cannot authenticate it. He is unable to bring witnesses who would confirm the signatures of the witnesses to the document.
and it is confirmed from his own mouth. By virtue of his admission.
and if the lender authenticated it afterward in court, it is like other documents. And its law is as above, halakhah 3.
that he broke. Canceled.

even though the lender is the one who broke his document. And it would seem he had grounds to claim that he should be believed, for had he wished to lie he would have claimed that this document is valid (the 'migo' argument).
he collects nothing with it, etc.. He admitted that this document is not valid, and therefore no money may be taken on the basis of this document.
it is considered like a potsherd. Like clay, and it has no significance at all.
he may not borrow with it again. The document cannot be used for a new loan.
for its lien was already released. The lien of this loan was voided with the repayment.
the document is void, etc.. And its law is as above, halakhah 6.
I returned the money to you because it was not good... the document is not void. For it is still the same loan.
but he did not mention the document to him. According to the testimony, at the time of repayment it was not stated that it was for the loan in the document.
the document is void. Since it is known that he repaid him a debt and we do not know of another debt.
the matters never occurred. And he denied what the witnesses said.
he is established as a liar. For his claim was contradicted by the witnesses.
for he did not repay him before witnesses. Rather, he only gave him before witnesses (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 6:2).
but is this document not the price of an ox I bought from you?. This promissory note is for an ox that I bought from you.
and you collected the price of its flesh. You collected the debt from the price of the ox's meat when it was sold in the slaughterhouse after slaughter.
for another debt. For a different debt.

since he himself admitted that the price of the ox is the debt, and from its price he paid. He admitted that the promissory note is for the price of the ox, and also admitted that he paid some debt from the price of the ox.

even though there are no witnesses that he paid from its price. Although no witnesses testify that he paid the debt from the meat of the ox, since he admitted that he paid the price of the ox, he is not believed to claim that he paid a different debt (Lechem Mishneh).
with one witness. Who signed on it, a single witness.

he is liable to an oath and cannot swear, and pays. One witness testifying to a monetary obligation obligates the defendant to a Torah-level oath (Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:1). And since the witness testifies about the promissory note, the borrower must swear against the witness's words in order to be exempt from payment. However, since the testimony is about the very fact of the loan, and the defendant does not contradict the witness but makes a different claim, he cannot swear against him and must pay (see also ibid. 4:8).
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 2.
he is liable to an oath. That he did not borrow.
and he cannot swear. For he agrees with the witness's words and makes a different claim in order to be exempt.
and he said, 'Let the lender swear and collect'. As above, halakhah 2.
bring his money. The repayment money.
and afterward he swears and collects. For if he swears and afterward the borrower cannot pay, it turns out that he swore for nothing.
they make him swear first, by the enactment of the Geonim, that he has nothing. See above 2:2.
and when he is able and gives to his creditor, etc.. When he has money and comes to pay his creditor, they make him swear first and then he gives him the money.

even though they made a kinyan from him, etc.. Even though, had there been no document at all, the witnesses could have written a document on the strength of the kinyan (above 11:1), in a case where a document was written a new document is not written. For we suspect that the borrower paid the debt and the lender tore up the document, which is why it is not in his possession.
he swears a heset oath. And is exempt.
and the time for its collection has not yet arrived. And we generally say that there is a presumption that a person does not repay before the repayment date.
that comes out from the hand of another. Found in the hands of a third person.
there is no presumption there. That he does not repay before the repayment date.
this one swears that he has no less than half of these monies, etc.. Like the law of an object that two people hold and each claims ownership of (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 9:7).
and if he cannot authenticate it, etc.. As above, halakhah 5.
swear to me a heset oath. Like one who denies everything.
and afterward you will produce the document, etc.. And it turns out he swore in vain.
they say to him. The court says to the lender.
or he had a document and it was lost. The lender claims that he lost his document.
nullify every document you have. Against the borrower, so that he can swear without concern.
or place a plain ban. If he does not wish to nullify his documents, he may place a ban on one who owes him and does not repay his debt, but he cannot make him swear.
stand with him. Are present before him in order to testify.
one who lends to his fellow before witnesses. Only, without a document.

there are versions, etc.. The laws that Rambam brought in the previous halakhah contradict the view of his teachers, Rif and R. Yosef ibn Migash (see Rif, Shevuot 21a-b in the Rif pages, and Ri Migash, Shevuot 41b), and Rambam proves his position from the versions of the Gemara and from logic.
I investigated the old versions. I checked what the reading is in the text of the old books.
the scrolls. A type of parchment.
close to five hundred years before this time. At the beginning of the Geonic period.
and I found two versions among the scrolls on this halakhah. Two copies that contain the Gemara that deals with this law.
and because of this error that occurred in some of the books, etc.. On the basis of the first ruling, which stemmed from an error in the reading, some Geonim ruled an additional law.

that he is not believed even though he brought the witnesses that he repaid him in their presence. According to them, when he stipulated that he would be repaid before certain witnesses, he disqualified all other people from serving as witnesses in this loan, and even if other witnesses come, he must repay the debt again as he stipulated.
this ruling too is according to their books. This ruling did not stem only from the previous error but also from an additional error in their books.

for it is written in them, regarding one who said to his fellow, 'Repay me before witnesses who have learned halakhot,' and he went and repaid him before witnesses. In the case brought in the Talmud (Shevuot 41b), the lender stipulated that the loan be repaid before sages who had studied halakhot, and the borrower repaid not as agreed, and from the Gemara's discussion it emerges that in this case the borrower is not believed when he claims that he paid. The versions differ as to exactly how the borrower paid: according to the version of some Geonim, the loan was returned before witnesses but they were not sages, from which it follows that if he stipulated repayment before certain witnesses, others are disqualified from testifying. According to Rambam's version, however, the repayment was not made before witnesses at all, which is why the borrower was not believed to claim that he paid. But if there are witnesses, even if they are not those he stipulated, they are believed.
he went and repaid him between himself and him. 'He went and repaid him privately,' and there are no witnesses to this.

even though the corrected books are as we said, this is also how it appears from the way of the Talmud. Not only is this the reading in the verified books, but this is also how it appears from the Gemara's words.
and furthermore, these are matters of reason. Logic also indicates this.
if so. If indeed he will not be believed in this claim.
this becomes testimony by document. It turns out that such a loan is treated like a loan by a document, in which the borrower must prove that he repaid the debt.
he caused the loss to himself. The borrower brought the loss upon himself.
there is no ground for suspicion here. There is no basis to suspect that he remains owing.
and in this manner it is fitting to judge and to rule. In this way.
that he be believed. The lender.
he collects without an oath, even though he claimed that he repaid him. And he cannot obligate him to swear in the manner explained above 14:2.
if he brought witnesses that he repaid him, he collects nothing. Because the trust applies only against the borrower's claim and not against witnesses of repayment.
for two are like a hundred. For in the laws of testimony, two witnesses have the same credibility as a hundred (see Hilchot Edut 18:3).

since he went down to the number, if he repaid him before four, it is paid. If his being believed were only to treat him as witnesses, he would not have been precise in stating a specific number; since he was precise to state a number, it implies that he was not believed against a larger number of witnesses.
what will be his remedy. How will he be exempt from the debt.

or he testifies about himself not in the presence of the borrower. For if the admission is made before the borrower, he could later cancel it and claim that he has two debts with this borrower, this debt for which he is believed as two witnesses and another oral debt, and only in order to collect the oral debt from him did he admit that he is receiving payment for this debt (Marcheshet Mishneh).
because I repaid you twice. The same debt.

he does not collect with this document, neither from the heir nor from the buyer. For the court argues on their behalf whatever the borrower could have argued, and since the borrower is believed in this claim, they too are exempt (Maggid Mishneh).

the lender does not seize with this document from buyers, lest they collude regarding this one's property. For fear that the lender and the borrower made a fraudulent agreement between them to claim that the debt was not repaid, so that the lender could seize land the borrower sold to others and they would divide the money between them.
the borrower claimed regarding this document. The lender sued the borrower by means of a promissory note.
a heset oath. And not the oath of one who admits part of a claim.
but if he comes to collect from his heirs. If the borrower died.
he swears and afterward collects. For the stipulation does not apply to collection from the heirs.
the best land. Superior land.
he came to collect from a buyer, he seizes only with an oath. Even if it was agreed that he would be believed without an oath even against buyers.
for he is not stipulating to destroy his fellow's money. The borrower is not permitted to make a condition that harms the rights of others.
his agent. An agent appointed by the lender to receive the debt payment.
he said to him, 'Throw my debt to me in the manner of a get'. According to the rules of delivery of a get (see Hilchot Gerushin 5:13-15).
if they were close to the borrower, they are still his responsibility. For in divorce, if he threw a get and it fell in a place closer to him than to her, she is not divorced.
if it was close to the lender, the borrower is exempt. For in divorce, when the get fell close to her, she is divorced.
half and half. In the middle of the distance between them.
if they were lost or stolen from there, the borrower pays half. And in divorce, in this case, it is uncertain whether she is divorced.
take to Shimon this maneh that I owe him. You will be an agent to return the debt to him.
if he comes to retract. If the borrower wants to retract from the giving to the agent.
he cannot retract. He may not retract, since the agent acquired the maneh on behalf of the lender.
and he is responsible for it until the maneh reaches Shimon. Although he cannot retract, the responsibility is on him and not on the lender, since he appointed the agent.
both are responsible for it. The agent too, since he improperly returned the maneh that the lender had already acquired.
give it to Levi. In payment of Shimon's debt to Levi.
and the three of them were standing. Together (see Hilchot Mekhirah 6:8).
and Levi accepted. He agreed that Reuven would be obligated to him in place of Shimon.
and Reuven was found to be poor and has nothing from which to collect. It turned out that Levi has no way to collect his debt from Reuven.
Levi returns to his debt against Shimon. Levi may again demand that Shimon repay his debt.
for he accepted. That Levi agreed, and therefore the debt that Shimon owed Reuven was acquired by Levi and Shimon was released from his debt to Levi.
Levi claimed that Reuven was poor and he misled him. Shimon, and that the acquisition was an acquisition made in error and Shimon still owes him.
and Shimon says, 'He was wealthy and became poor'. And that he did not mislead him.

he is no more than one holding a receipt, etc.. For even if he has a receipt for the repayment, he must prove its authenticity in order to be exempt. Therefore here too, where he claims to be released from responsibility for payment, he must prove it.
in Hilchot Mekach u-Mimkar. Hilchot Mekhirah 6:9.
for Reuven had nothing with Shimon. That Shimon did not owe him money.
and he assigned him to Shimon. They agreed in the presence of the three of them that Levi would collect from Shimon what Reuven owed him, and Reuven would pay Shimon at a later date.

even though he assigned him in the presence of the three of them, he did not acquire. For the law mentioned in the previous halakhah is a unique law that applies only when the person with whom the money was assigned owed money to the borrower who assigned it, and not in other cases (ibid. 5:8).
and if Shimon wishes not to give, he need not give. Shimon is not obligated to give Levi payment of Reuven's debt even though they agreed so.
and if he gave. If Shimon nevertheless gave to Levi.
he returns and collects from Reuven, for it was at his word that he gave. And Reuven obligated himself to repay him what he would give to Levi.
and he keeps him on credit until it all accumulates. He postpones collecting payment until a certain sum accumulates, and then the householder pays him everything.
give my worker a sela, etc.. He asks the shopkeeper to pay his worker or his creditor, and he will repay him when he settles the credit account.
and the shopkeeper says, 'I gave'. To the worker or the creditor as agreed.
I did not take. From the shopkeeper, and he claims that the householder must pay him.

the worker or creditor swears and collects. For the householder does not know whether the shopkeeper paid or not. He admits that he owed them and claims that perhaps he already paid his debt, while they make a definite claim that he still owes them.
for he told him to give. Since he did not require him to give before witnesses, he trusted him to give and obligated himself to pay him for it (see Bavli Bava Metzia 3a).
so that they will be ashamed of each other. And whoever is lying may perhaps confess and avoid a false oath.

and this oath is an enactment of the Sages, while holding a sacred object, because both come to collect. By strict law they need not swear at all, but the Sages instituted that they swear because the householder loses from both parties collecting from him.

therefore if the shopkeeper died, the creditor collects without an oath, etc.. The oath obligation arises because he must pay both; therefore when one of them dies and does not claim, the other does not swear at all.
the householder swears a heset oath and is exempt. Like one who denies everything (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:3).
to the householder who keeps him on credit. Who is accustomed to buy from him on credit.
it is written in my ledger that you owe me a maneh. That you owe me a maneh.

like the law of anyone who claims against his fellow in any matter. Like one who sues his fellow, and the defendant says he does not know whether he ever obligated himself to him (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:8).
and there is no enactment of the Sages here. That he swear while holding a sacred object.

and he claimed that Levi gave it to him by writing and delivery, and the document by which he transferred it was lost. In the acquisition of a promissory note, it is not enough to deliver the document to the buyer; one must also add the writing of a document in which the creditor transfers the lien of the note to the buyer (see Hilchot Mekhirah 6:11).
or he claimed that he transferred it to him together with land. For if he transfers the document through acquisition together with land, no writing is needed (ibid. 6:14).

he collects it from Shimon, since it came out from his possession. It is reasonable that it truly is his, and he need not bring witnesses about the purchase of the document. However, if Shimon claims that he does not believe Reuven that Levi transferred it to him, Reuven must bring proof in order to collect the debt (Hilchot Mekhirah 6:11).
and he said, 'Let him swear to me,' Levi swears. For when the borrower claims that he paid and wants the lender to swear to him that his debt was not repaid, the lender is made to swear (above 14:2).
he admitted to him that he was paid. Levi admits that he received payment of the debt from Shimon.
Levi claimed that he did not sell or give this document. Levi claims that although he collected the debt, he did not sell or give the document as a gift to Reuven and he does not owe him payment.
he swears a heset oath and is exempt. Like one who denies everything.
a third party. A third person who serves as trustee of the document.
even though the document is authenticated. Whose signatures were examined and confirmed in court, and had it been in the lender's hand the borrower could not claim that he paid the debt.

and a writing was found coming from the hand of the third party that this document deposited with him is paid. They found that the third party had a document stating that the note deposited with him is paid.
it is no more than as one joking. And it should not be treated as an admission.
there were witnesses on the writing. There is a signature of witnesses on the written repayment of the document that the lender wrote.
if they were authenticated. If the document bears a court's confirmation attesting to the witnesses' signatures.
the document is paid. For the fact that they went to the trouble of authenticating the receipt shows that it is serious.
the witnesses are asked. Whether they saw the repayment, or signed the receipt at the lender's request without having seen that his debt was paid.
the document was found, etc.. If the same document on which there is a writing that it is paid was found among the lender's paid documents, presumably it too is paid.
and likewise if it was found written on the body of the document. On the document itself, and not in a separate writing.
on its front... on its back. On the front or back side of the document.
at its edge. At the margin of the document.
they act according to the writing. Even if it is not placed among the paid documents.
and it is not known what its nature is. Whether the debt written in it was already collected.
until Elijah comes. And clarifies the matter.
one who says to his sons, etc.. And afterward died.
a document among my documents. One of my documents.
all his documents are paid. No document can be collected.
two were found with one person. If there are two documents against the same borrower.

the large one is paid and the small one is not paid. Since he admitted only one document, certainly one of this person's documents is not paid, so the document with the larger sum is considered paid, and they may collect the document with the smaller sum.
he said to his fellow, 'Your document in my hand is paid'. And he has two documents against him.
a debt of yours in my hand is paid. And he did not refer to documents.
the documents he has against him are all paid. Since it is possible that his intention is that he has no debt against him at all.
he said, 'Let him swear to me'. That he really does not know.
he swears. Just as their father would have been obligated to swear against the claim of repayment had the borrower demanded it (above 14:2).
that Father did not instruct us through another... that this document is paid. That he did not inform us through a third person that the document is paid.
and that we did not find among Father's documents that this document is paid. As above 16:10.
he collects only with an oath. For one collects from heirs only with an oath (above 14:1).
and even if the heir was. The lender's heir.
he swears and collects. After he grows up.
as we have explained. Above 14:1.

and a person does not bequeath an oath to his sons, etc.. Money that a person can receive only by means of an oath cannot be bequeathed to his sons. For the sons cannot take the oath that their father already obligated himself to, since he obligated himself to swear that this document is not paid, and they cannot swear this with certainty (for they cannot know all their father's affairs). And their oath 'that Father did not instruct us,' etc., is not sufficient, because there is an obligation of a different oath here (Rashi, Shevuot 47a).
they do not take it out of their hands. Since there is no definitive ruling in this halakhah (see Bavli Shevuot 48b).
therefore. Since after the fact, if the lender's heirs collected, it is not taken out of their hands.
as we have explained. In the previous paragraph.
and the borrower died first. And one cannot collect from his heirs.
the lender's heirs do not collect from the guarantor. Even though their father could have collected from him even without an oath.
the guarantor then returns and collects from the borrower's heirs. By the law of a guarantor (below 26:6), and it turns out that in the end they are collected from.

one does not derive from this law to anything similar to it. Since there is no clear ruling in this law (as explained above, halakhah 3), the Sages said that one should not extrapolate from it to other cases in which the lender was obligated to swear and died.
one who impairs his document and dies. A lender who admitted that part of the debt is paid, whose law is that he collects only with an oath (above 14:1), and who died before swearing.
the lender's heirs collect without an oath. Even if the borrower died during the lender's lifetime.

for anyone who says 'I did not borrow' is like one who says 'I did not repay'. For if he did not borrow from him, certainly he did not repay him, and since the lender's heirs have a document proving the very debt, they can collect it without an oath.
even if he trusted him in the document, whenever he says 'I paid'. Even if it was agreed in the document that the borrower would be believed to claim that the document is paid (see above 15:6).
for anyone who says 'I did not borrow' is like one who says 'I did not repay'. And it turns out that the borrower admitted that he did not repay the debt.

the borrower swears a heset oath that he paid this document, and is exempt. Since it was stipulated that the borrower would be believed to claim that he paid, the heir cannot collect his debt from him by means of the document. But the borrower must swear a heset oath, for the stipulation gives him credibility against the document but does not exempt him from a heset oath (see above 15:6).

for the essence of the document was on this condition. Since the document was written essentially on the condition that the borrower would be believed to claim that he paid, the loan does not have the force of a loan by a document that must be repaid before witnesses, but is like an oral loan in which the borrower is always believed to claim that he paid, even against the lender's heirs.
and if he stipulated with him. If he stipulated that he would be believed also in this respect, that he would not be liable to a heset oath (see there).
a receipt. A writing that releases the borrower from the debt.
they do not tear up the document. Even though there is a receipt on it.
and they do not collect with it. The debt cannot be collected, since a receipt has been issued against it.
until the orphans grow up. And perhaps they will then bring proof against the receipt.
and therefore the borrower did not produce it during the father's lifetime. For fear of making a false claim in his presence.

one who produces a promissory note against his fellow. If the document does not state in whose place's currency the loan was made, and in different places the same type of coin has a different value (for example, a Babylonian dinar is not equal in value to an Israeli dinar).
and it was written in Babylonia. The document states that it was written in Babylonia.
whereas this is not so with a ketubah. For in payment of a ketubah to a woman, she is always given the currency of lower value (see Hilchot Ishut 16:6).
and he produced it in Babylonia. He produced the document in Babylonia in order to collect with it.
he comes to collect with it in the currency of the place where the document was issued. When the place was not written in the document.
for the money I owe him is from silver that is less than this coin. The obligation was in a coin worth less than the coin of this place.
if it said plain silver. If the document states that the debt is in silver coins but does not state which type of coin is meant.
for a document that has no place name... is valid. Unlike a get, which is invalid if the place and date are not stated in it (see Hilchot Gerushin 1:25).
date. The calendar date.

even though you cannot refute this testimony. That is, refuting witnesses cannot say that on that day the witnesses were with them in another place, and by strict law such testimony is not valid (see Hilchot Edut 1:5).
as will be explained. See there 3:1.
so that a door not be locked before borrowers. So that people not refrain from lending to one another because of the need to undergo meticulous clarification if the borrower denies the loan.
therefore. Since they are not particular about writing the date in the document.
post-dated promissory notes are valid. But pre-dated ones are invalid.
as will be explained in its place. Below 23:2.
one who lends to his fellow without specification. With a general lien on his property, without designating a specific asset for collection.

all his property is responsible and guaranteeing for this debt. When a person does not repay his debt with money, his property is responsible for repayment of the debt (similar to one who guaranteed his fellow's debt and must pay when the borrower does not pay).
both movable property and land. However, when he has movable property he cannot pay with land (see above 1:4, and see there in Piskei u-Shitot whether he can pay with movables when he has money).
the court collects it for him. For the order of collection see below chapter 22.
he collects from all the land the borrower had. At the time of the loan, for land is mortgaged by Torah law to the debt even when it is no longer in the borrower's possession (above 11:7).

he takes it from the hands of buyers or recipients of gifts, and this is called seizing. Seizure from buyers is done only for a lender by a document (see above 11:4). And when a creditor seizes land (or movables) from the buyer, the buyer can go back and claim from the seller the money he paid him, since in general the seller bears responsibility for what he sold (see Hilchot Mekhirah 19:3 and above 11:5; and see Hilchot Shekhenim 13:1 and below 20:3 that in a gift the giver does not ordinarily take responsibility unless he says so explicitly).
property that comes to him after he borrowed. That he acquired or gained after he borrowed.

is not mortgaged to his creditor, and he does not seize it. He does not take it from the hands of buyers or recipients of gifts (but if it is in his own possession, the creditor does collect from it, as explained at the beginning of the halakhah, that all property in the borrower's hands is responsible and guaranteeing for the debt).
but movable property has no responsibility. For by Torah law only the lender's land is mortgaged to the debt, but not his movable property (above 11:7).

even movables that he sold at once, the creditor does not seize them. Even if he sold them immediately after the loan (= 'le-sha'ato' - compare the wording in Hilchot Shabbat 9:13), he does not collect from them, even though one could argue that he is scheming to sell in order to remove them from the creditor (Yad Peshutah, following Meromei Sadeh).

he transferred to his creditor all his movables together with the land. He transferred the movables to him so that they would be mortgaged to repay the debt, and did so along with transferring the land as a lien for repayment of his debt.
not as an asmakhta. A term for a future commitment that is not binding because of a lack of firm intent (see Hilchot Mekhirah 11:2).
and not like the forms of documents. Documents written as a sample or for another reason, which have no validity (and see Rashba, Bava Batra 44b on why these details must be stated).

he made his field an apotiki. He designated it for collection of his debt (the word's origin is Greek, meaning pledge, a mortgaged asset; and in his Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 4:4 he interpreted the word as a combination of the words 'peh tikanah'; for the implications of making an apotiki see below halakhah 4, halakhah 8, 21:6-7, and Piskei u-Shitot here).
and a river swept it away. It covered it and it cannot be used.
he collects from other property. For designating the field does not remove the lien from other property.
and if he stipulated with him that he would have no repayment except from this one. And thereby designated it more than an ordinary apotiki.
and specified that he has no responsibility for it. That they explicitly stipulated that he does not mortgage to the loan his property that he will sell or give to others.
for the time being. For a limited time.
but if he sold it as a permanent sale, it is not sold. Since it is mortgaged to the lender or to the woman's ketubah, it cannot be transferred entirely to another's ownership.
the creditor collects from him. From the buyer.
because it has publicity. There is publicity that it was mortgaged to the debt, and the buyer should have refrained from buying it (compare above 11:4).
his master. His owner.
even though he wrote to him, 'You will have no repayment except from this'. And he mortgaged it to him with a full lien that repayment of the debt would be specifically from it.
and likewise if he consecrated it. See below halakhah 7.

for chametz... removes from the lien. If he borrowed from a gentile and designated chametz food for repayment, when Pesach arrives the prohibition of chametz removes the lien held by the gentile and it returns to Israelite ownership and is forbidden for benefit and must be destroyed.
and he writes a document for him for his debt. The lender writes the borrower a new promissory note for this loss, for now the debt has been voided because the slave went free.
