and he seizes from the time of this document. If the lender comes to collect from the borrower's buyers with the second document, he collects only from what was sold after the document was written and not from the time of the original loan.
as we explained in its place. Hilchot Chovel u-Mazik 7:7.
and they compel his second master to free him, etc.. See also there halakhah 11, Hilchot Avadim 8:16.
one who consecrates his property. To the Temple.

and when the land is redeemed from the hands of the Temple treasury. When the Temple treasurers take the land out for sale and the redeemer pays its value to the Temple treasury and the land becomes non-sacred.

they say, etc.. When announcing the sale of the land, they announce in advance that after the redemption the wife or the creditor will collect their debt from the land, and only the remainder will belong to the buyer.

because when it is redeemed and goes out to non-sacred status in the buyer's hands, a creditor will come and seize it, etc.. For the lien that was suspended by the consecration was not voided, and it returns to force after the redemption.
as we have explained in Arakhin. Hilchot Arakhin va-Charamin 7:14-16.
and the buyer returns and claims from the seller. As with a buyer from whom property was seized.
for a maneh. One hundred dinars.
and he seized one for a maneh. For half of the debt.

if you wish the field you seized to be valued for you at the full two hundred that you are owed, etc.. The buyer can present the creditor with a choice between two options: either the field he seized for one hundred will be considered worth two hundred and will be repayment of the entire debt, or he will return it to him and the buyer will pay the entire two hundred in the borrower's place.
here, two hundred of your debt, and withdraw. For the buyer can pay off the creditor with money, as explained in the previous halakhah.
Shimon wished and stood by it. He agreed to be satisfied with the field he took in place of the two-hundred debt.

Levi may claim only one maneh. Even though Shimon took the field for the debt of two hundred, Levi can claim from Reuven, who sold him the field, only one maneh, since the field's value is indeed one maneh.
and Shimon came and seized it. And a further hundred of the debt remained.

for the hundred they gave him was a mitzvah they performed, etc.. Ordinarily, when the buyer pays the creditor and removes him from the field, it is as if he buys it from him and the lien on it is voided. But in the case discussed here, the creditor can claim that the hundred the orphans gave him was not to remove him from the land but to repay their father's debt. Thus, according to his claim, the field is still mortgaged to his debt.
for it is a mitzvah for orphans to repay their father's debt. As above 11:8 (and the discussion here is from before the Geonic enactment to collect from movables as well - Shakh 107:9).

and if they said to him, 'This hundred is the price of the field you seized'. If they said explicitly that the hundred they are giving him is not for repayment of their father's debt but to remove him from the land he seized.
only from the middling among his lands. Lands are divided basically into three grades: best, middling, and poorest.
and the law of the Torah is that a creditor collects from the poorest. By strict law a creditor collects from the borrower's poor and weak land, called zibburit.

as it is stated, 'You shall stand outside, and the man, etc.'. The verse speaks of taking a pledge from a borrower, and says that the lender stands outside, 'and the man to whom you lend shall bring the pledge outside to you,' meaning the borrower decides what to bring out to the lender. Presumably he brings out something inferior, and so the court also collects this way.

so that a door not be locked before borrowers. For if lenders were to receive from borrowers their poorest land, they might refrain from lending to them; therefore for the benefit of borrowers they enacted that the lender collect from the middling.
he collects only from the poorest. In these cases the Sages did not enact that he collect from the middling.

one does not collect from mortgaged property where there is free property. When there is property in the borrower's possession ('free property'), one does not collect from property that is not now in his possession but is mortgaged to the debt.
whether he gave them. As a gift.
they deteriorated. They spoiled until they yield nothing.
for once they were ruined it is as if they do not exist. And when he has no free property in his hands, one collects from the mortgaged property.
and Shimon went and sold one field to Levi. Of those fields he bought from Reuven.

if he wishes he collects from this one, if he wishes he collects from that one. The creditor may choose to collect his debt from Shimon, for he bought all the land of Reuven the debtor and stepped into his place regarding the lien. He may also choose to collect from Levi in certain cases, as explained shortly.
where Levi bought middling land. From which by strict law one collects, as above, halakhah 1.

for this reason I went to the trouble and bought a field from which it is not your right to collect. I deliberately bought this field specifically, and left with Shimon the field from which it is your right to collect.
for he says to him, 'I left you a place from which to collect'. From the middling land in Shimon's hands.
we have already explained that those who were damaged are assessed from the best. A person damaged by his fellow collects from the best of his fellow's property (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 8:10).
and a creditor from the middling. Above, halakhah 1.
and a woman's ketubah from the poorest. Hilchot Ishut 16:3.

if he had best and poorest, etc.. The principle is that if one cannot collect the land that is due by law, he collects inferior land and cannot collect better land (and the case is, for example, where the debtor initially had best, middling, and poorest land, and after incurring the debt sold one of them, so the remaining lands may be best and middling or middling and poorest, since they assess according to the quality of the borrower's lands, as explained above, halakhah 1 - Kesef Mishneh).
he sold them to three people. Each one land of a different type.
at once. Simultaneously.
all of them entered in place of the owner. All the lands they bought are mortgaged to the same type of debt as when in the seller's hands, and each creditor collects according to his due.
he sold them one after another. He sold to several buyers at different times.
all of them seize from the last. They collect from the last buyer, since he did not leave enough property with the debtor to collect from.
it was not sufficient. The property he bought was not enough to cover the entire debt.
from the one before him. From the first buyer.
even if the last was the one who bought the poorest. Even though the damaged party and the lender lose by this, all collect poorest land.
the earlier buyer. Who bought earlier from the owner.
I left you a place from which to collect. For when he bought the land, the owner still had other property from which the creditor could collect.
this buyer enters in place of the owner. And each creditor collects according to his due.
I left you a place from which to collect. For the poorest land was still free when he bought the better lands from it, and therefore it takes precedence for collection.

and why does the seizer not say to him the same, if he bought the best last, etc.. For just as the buyer can claim that they should seize from him in order of purchase, and collect only from the poorest, so too the seizer can use the same argument and claim that his right is to collect from the land purchased last, since it was free when the others had already been sold.

for this is an enactment for the buyer. For by strict law the order of purchase of lands has no significance, and the creditor was permitted to collect from the earlier buyers. The Sages enacted for the benefit of buyers that whoever left a place to collect from in free lands is not collected from first.
and he says to them, 'I do not want this enactment, etc.'. The buyer may waive the enactment, because it works against him when he bought the best land last.

for he has nothing with which to push them off. Since he bought the best land last, the creditors collect from it, because by the Sages' enactment they collect from the last land remaining in the debtor's possession. In this case the buyer cannot claim that he does not want the Sages' enactment, since the waiver relies on all the debtor's lands being in his hand, and here the middling and poorest lands are no longer his but in others' hands (see Meiri, Bava Kamma 8b).
he sold the best and left middling and poorest. The first buyer sold the best land he bought last and kept the middling and poorest in his possession.

the damaged parties seize from the best in the hand of the second buyer, etc.. For the second buyer bought from the first the rights he had in the land. And just as the first buyer can waive the Sages' enactment when all the lands were in his hand and give each one his due (as above, halakhah 6), so can the second buyer (Bavli ibid.).
and afterward the borrower sold his property to two. At different times.
I have no dispute or claims with you. And he removed the lien he has on him in the collection of this debt.
and they made a kinyan from him. They performed a kinyan sudar to remove the lien (see Hilchot Mekhirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
I left you a place from which to collect from your debtor, etc.. For when he bought the borrower's property he left with him property from which the debt could be collected.
and the same applies to a woman for her ketubah. Where her husband sold his property mortgaged to her ketubah to two buyers at different times.

but if they wrote to the first, they seize from the second. Although the creditors removed the lien from the first buyer's property, the lien remains on the property the second buyer bought, and therefore they can seize from him.
and afterward he sold a second field to a second buyer. And the debt is equal to the value of both fields together, as explained at the end of the halakhah.

and the first buyer seizes the second field from the second buyer. When the lender seized from the first buyer, the seller became obligated to him, and the first buyer can collect his claim from the field in the second buyer's hands, which is mortgaged to his debt.

and the second buyer takes it out from the creditor, for he wrote to him. For after the first buyer seized the field from the second buyer, the creditor can seize from him the field, since his debt preceded the buyer's debt (see below 20:1). And since the second buyer's field is now in the creditor's hands, the second buyer can take it out of the creditor's hands, for he removed the lien he had on this buyer.
and the first buyer returns and seizes from the second. The land that he took from the creditor.
and they go round and round until they make a compromise between them. This situation repeats cyclically and has no halakhic solution until they reach a compromise agreement.
one who has many debts. To different people, and he does not have enough to repay all his debts.

whether from the borrower himself or from the buyers. Whether the debt is collected directly from the borrower or from mortgaged property in the hands of buyers, priority goes to the one whose debt came first.
in the lands he had at the time he borrowed. These were mortgaged at the time of the loan, and therefore whoever lent first has priority in his lien.
even though he wrote to each of them, 'What I will acquire in the future is mortgaged to you'. In this way, even lands he acquired later become mortgaged to the lender (above 18:2).

there is no law of priority among them. Since the lien took effect on them at the time of acquisition, when he was already obligated to all of them, the earlier lenders have no advantage over the later ones.
the field is mortgaged to the first. Since it was mortgaged to the first at the time it was acquired, and to the second only afterward when he borrowed from him.
and likewise even if there were a hundred. The laws of priority apply in the same way whether there were two creditors or a hundred.
one of the others got ahead. Someone who is not a creditor of the borrower.

and likewise if the borrower said to him, etc.. If the other person did not seize on his own, but the borrower told him to acquire on behalf of one of the lenders, he acquires it for him even if there are other creditors whose loans came first. For in this case it is the borrower who transfers the movables to the lender, only that he does so through another person, since 'acquire' and 'give' are expressions of transfer (see Hilchot Zekhiyah u-Matanah 4:4).
for their dates are all the same day. And in that place they do not state the time of the loan in the document, and one cannot tell from them which debt came first.
whichever of them got ahead and collected... acquired. As with two who borrowed at the same time.
if when the available property is divided according to their number. If the assets are divided equally according to the number of creditors.
it reaches the smallest of them in the amount of his debt. The lender who is owed the least receives his full debt.

and the remaining creditors return and divide the surplus among themselves in the same manner. They divide again equally up to the amount of the next-lowest debt, and then the balance passes to the creditors of larger debts.
a maneh. One hundred zuz.
they each take one hundred. Each collects one hundred.

and there are Geonim who ruled that they divide according to their money. In their view everything is divided in proportion to the size of the debt. For example, in the case under discussion where the total of the debts reaches one thousand, one who is owed one hundred takes a tenth of the borrower's property, one who is owed two hundred takes two tenths, and one who is owed seven hundred takes seven tenths.

and I lean toward this for movables. When collecting from land, which is subject to a lien on property, they divide equally since each of the creditors has a lien on all the borrower's property, and so their strength is equal. But when collecting from movables, on which there is no lien, one whose debt is larger is entitled to a larger share in the collection (based on Yad Peshutah).
they all came together to collect. Holders of documents of equal date.

how do they divide?. In all the cases mentioned, none of the creditors has priority over another and they divide equally. However, when the borrower owes a different sum to each of them and does not have enough property to pay everyone, it must be determined in what manner the money is divided among them.

and Shimon's document is dated 'Nisan' without specification. The document states only in which month he lent to him, without the exact day, and it is not known whether it was written before Reuven's document or after it.
they let Reuven descend into it. The court has Reuven collect it.
perhaps Shimon's document was from the end of Nisan. And he must prove that his document came before Reuven's document.
and likewise Shimon cannot seize from Iyar onward. If the borrower sold other land in Iyar, even though it certainly was sold after he borrowed from Shimon, Shimon cannot seize it from the buyer.

for the buyer says to him, etc.. The buyer rebuffs him with the claim that he is not the one entitled to seize from him, for perhaps his document precedes Reuven's document, in which case he should have seized the free land that Reuven seized, and only Reuven has the right to seize from the buyer.

therefore if they wrote an authorization for each other, they seize from Iyar onward from either side. Reuven and Shimon may write a document in which each empowers the other to claim his debt on his behalf, and then each of them is the agent of the other and collects the land from the buyer, whether by virtue of Reuven or by virtue of Shimon (see Hilchot Sheluchin ve-Shutafin 3:1).

and the same applies to Reuven and Shimon, to whom Levi sold one field by two documents, etc.. If he sold the same field to both of them and it is not known who acquired it first, the one whose document states the fifth of Nisan precedes his fellow, unless the other proves that his document came first.

a creditor collects the improvement that the buyer made. A lender who comes to collect land from someone who bought it from the borrower also collects from what the buyer improved in the land, and not only from the value of the land itself without the improvement.
whether he improved it through expense. That the buyer invested and spent money for the improvement.
he collects half the improvement. And the other half remains with the buyer.
for a maneh. One hundred dinars.
and if it improved on its own. And it is now worth two hundred.
that it rose in price. That it became more expensive without changing.
or trees grew in it. Grew on their own.

the buyer should not be in a worse position than one who goes down into his fellow's field without permission. It is not reasonable that the buyer's status be lower than that of one who works his fellow's field without permission and improves it, where the investment and the value of the improvement are assessed and the owner pays him the lesser of the two (Hilchot Gezelah 10:4). Therefore here too the buyer must be given what he invested in the field, and afterward the buyer and the creditor divide the remaining improvement between them.

and the buyer returns and collects the principal from Shimon's property, even from mortgaged property. The seller bears responsibility for the field he sold, and when it is taken from the buyer he must return the purchase price to him. The buyer can collect his debt from mortgaged property that was sold or given to others after he bought the field (see above 11:5).
whether half of it. If it improved through the buyer's investment.
or all of it. If it improved on its own.
for it is an enactment for the good of the world, etc.. The Sages enacted that in the cases mentioned here the debt is not collected from mortgaged property, for the good of the world.
that the improvement mentioned in the halakhah here not be collected. The improvement mentioned in this halakhah.

nor the produce that the robber ate. One who robbed a field and ate its produce must return the land and the value of the produce he ate. And this payment is collected only from the robber's free property (see Hilchot Gezelah 9:5).

nor the support of the wife and daughters. From the terms of the ketubah, the wife and daughters are supported from the property of the man who died until the daughters are betrothed or until the wife claims her ketubah and the daughters come of age (Hilchot Ishut 18:1, 19:10). And if he died and his heirs sold his property, they cannot seize it from the buyer for their support (see there 18:13).
for these are matters that have no fixed amount. Their value is not known in advance, and therefore those who buy these lands from the heirs cannot estimate the risk they are taking upon themselves.

and it is among the leniencies of the ketubah that a woman does not seize from the improvement for her ketubah. Although the ketubah itself is collected from mortgaged property (since it has a fixed amount), the Sages established that she cannot collect the ketubah money from the improvement that arose in the buyer's hands. This limitation is one of the matters in which the law of the ketubah is more lenient than the laws of other promissory notes (see there 16:5).
and why does a creditor seize only half of the improvement that came through expense?. And does not take all of it as he takes all of the principal.
and Reuven and Levi turn out to be two creditors of Shimon. Reuven the lender and Levi the buyer have the status of two creditors of Shimon.

and the improvement is among the property that came to him after he borrowed from both. The improvement has the status of property that came to the owner after he obligated himself to both [in some printings and manuscripts the reading is: 'and Reuven and Levi turn out to be like two... and the improvement like property...', and the meaning is the same].

for they divide as one, as we have explained. For the property is mortgaged to both creditors and is divided between them equally, as explained above 20:1 (and all this applies to an improvement that the buyer made, but an improvement that came on its own is not considered a new acquisition but part of the land that existed at the time of the loan and was mortgaged only to the lender, and therefore he takes all of it).
Shimon and Levi seize the principal and divide it equally. For the principal is mortgaged to both equally, since the land was acquired after the loan dates of both (see above 20:1).
and Shimon, Levi and Judah, the three of them, return and divide the hundred and fifty of improvement. For the improvement is also mortgaged to Judah.
in the manner we explained. Above 20:4, where it was explained how they divide when the borrower owes a different sum to several creditors and does not have enough money to pay them all.

it turns out, etc.. At first Shimon and Levi divide between them the hundred and fifty that the principal is worth, which is mortgaged only to them. Afterward the three of them divide the improvement among them.
Shimon seized his maneh from this field. Seventy-five from the principal, and another twenty-five from the improvement, since his share is limited to the amount of the loan.

and Levi seized one hundred thirty-seven and a half. Seventy-five from the principal, and another sixty-two and a half (which is twenty-five zuz in the first division among the three of them, plus thirty-seven and a half, which is half of the remainder, which he divides equally with Judah).
and Judah took from the improvement sixty-two and a half. For Judah took from the improvement only.
that the buyer ate. That he took from the field.
that had reached the time of harvesting. That had ripened and were ready to be harvested.
a creditor collects from them. Even though they no longer need the ground, they are not considered produce in the buyer's possession.
how much it was worth at the time of the gift. The land without the improvement.
and if the giver accepted responsibility for the gift. That if the field he received is taken from the recipient, the giver will pay him its value.
and why does he seize, etc.. What is the reason for the difference between a buyer and a gift recipient regarding seizure of the improvement.

and the buyer wished and accepted this matter, etc.. The buyer agreed to the seller's terms of responsibility, and he held the land on the understanding that the seller is responsible to pay him if the principal and the improvement are seized from him; hence seizing the improvement from the buyer is included in the agreement of the terms of sale.
and even if he did not write. Even if the seller did not write the buyer a responsibility for the sale.

it is already known that this is the law of the seller with the buyer. In a plain sale the seller takes on responsibility even if he did not write it explicitly (Hilchot Mekhirah 19:3). By contrast, in a gift there is no responsibility unless it is explicit in the document (see Hilchot Shekhenim 13:1).

and likewise orphans, etc.. Orphans who inherited land from their father, from whom their father's creditor comes to seize the land after they improved it, have a law similar to that of a gift recipient regarding seizure of improvement, since they too have no one from whom to take back what they invested.
benefit. Usefulness.

for example, if there remained for him in the field a beit tish'at kabin and in the garden a beit half-kav. A field is intended for extensive agricultural work, so if its area is too small to sow nine kavs it has no use as a field, whereas a garden, which is intended for limited agricultural work, requires at least an area for sowing half a kav (see Hilchot Shekhenim 1:4).
they both share in it. They use it as neighbors, each in his own portion.

and if nothing remains for him that, if divided, would still carry the whole name. If after the lender takes what is due to him, no part is left to the buyer that is still called by the former name of the thing before it was divided.
the creditor gives him its value. The creditor gives the value of the remaining part as compensation to the buyer, and all of it will be his.
if the field was an apotiki, etc.. If the borrower designated this land for collection of the debt (see above 18:3), the law of the improvement differs from the case of an ordinary lien.

the creditor takes all of it. Unlike the usual case, where the improvement is divided between the lender and the buyer because it is mortgaged to both equally (as above, halakhah 1), here the entire improvement belongs to the lender, since the field was designated for him for his debt, and it turns out that the whole improvement belongs to his field that improved.

and we consider half of the improvement that remains for the buyer, etc.. Although the entire improvement belongs to the lender, nevertheless it came about as a result of the buyer's investment, and therefore the lender must pay him for it. The buyer is treated like one who goes down into his fellow's field without permission, where the investment and the value of the improvement are assessed and the owner pays him the lesser of the two. However, in this case the reimbursement the buyer receives is limited to half of the improvement amount (see Yad Peshutah, who gave a reason for this, and it requires further study).
a creditor who came to seize from the orphans. For a debt that their father owed him.
the orphans say, 'We improved it'. And the improvement is not mortgaged to the debt.
and the creditor says, 'Perhaps your father improved it'. And he is entitled to receive the improvement for his debt.
we assess for them the improvement and the expense, etc.. They assess the value of the improvement and the expenses they spent on this improvement, and the orphans receive the lesser of the two.
and he pays them in money. He pays them money for that amount.

where he made this field an apotiki. Although ordinarily a creditor does not collect the improvement at all from orphans (as above, halakhah 4), if he made the field an apotiki it is his, and the orphans are treated like one who goes down into his fellow's field without permission, where the improvement and the expense are assessed and they take the lesser of the two.

but if he did not make it an apotiki, etc.. In this case the lender has no right in the land, and all the improvement is theirs. Therefore they may choose to give him money in the value of the land and remove him from it, or give him land minus the improvement they made in it (as above 18:8).
the order of collecting the debt. The stages of the collection procedure.
when the lender brings his document to court and it is authenticated. The court confirms the witnesses' signatures (for the manner of authenticating a document see Hilchot Edut chapter 6).

and they do not go down to his property at first until he claims it from him. The procedure of taking possession of the borrower's property does not begin with presenting the document, but only after the lender demands payment from the borrower and he does not pay him.

they remove him. The lender from the borrower's property (Rabbeinu Avraham, head of the court, on Bava Batra 174a, and so it implies from Ritva there). Some explain that they remove the judge from deciding (Rabbeinu Gershom and Meiri there).

either I will pledge or I will sell. From the lands in his possession. But from movables they collect immediately (and some wrote that even with movables, if the lender consented not to collect and gave him permission to sell them and pay from the proceeds, they give him thirty days - Yad Peshutah, following the responsa of the Rif, sec. 105 and sec. 271).
for had there been movables there, the court would have collected from them immediately. And so there is no possibility that the borrower has movables to give the lender as a pledge.

and if the lender wished to place a ban on whoever has money or movables. The lender may place a general ban on anyone who has the ability to pay money or movables and puts him off with excuses (see above 1:4).

an adrakhta. A document in which the court strengthens the plaintiff's power to collect from the defendant's property. 'Adrakhta' is from the language of pursuit, as in the verse 'they pursued him, they trod him down at rest' (Judges 20:43, and below halakhah 13 it is called 'hadrakhah').
and they do not fix a time for him. They do not give him thirty days, for he said he would not pay and there is no reason to give him time.

an oral loan or one he admitted. That he lent to him before witnesses or admitted before them that he owes him money. In these cases the debt is defined as an oral loan (above 11:1), and it is collected only from free property.
and with defective claims. Flawed claims with no substance.
pay, and afterward if you have proof, he will return it. The lender will return to you what you gave him.

and if the lender was an alam. A violent person who does not submit to the authority of the law, and there is concern that the defendant will not be able to collect his money back from him if he brings proof contradicting the document.
they place it with a third party. They give the repayment money to a third person who serves as trustee of the money until the final judgment.
they wait for him Monday, Thursday and Monday. For on these days courts convene to hear cases, and they wait for him three court days.
a petichah. A document of excommunication.
and they place him under a ban. They excommunicate, like the law of one who did not come at the time the court set for him (Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:14).
and they wait for him while he is under his ban. They still refrain from writing an adrakhta, but in the meantime he is excommunicated.

ninety days. Although above in halakhah 1 it was explained that one who asks for time to repay the loan is given only thirty days, after which an adrakhta is written on his property, in this case he is given ninety days because the borrower is not present before us now. But if he is present before us, in this case too he is given only thirty days (responsa of the Rif, sec. 206; and the Sema 98:11 explained that since he claimed the document is forged, his power is strengthened in this respect, so that he is given ninety days).
middle ones, perhaps he is going to the trouble of selling. After he did not find anyone to borrow from.
perhaps the buyer from him is going to the trouble of bringing money. Perhaps the person who bought from him is making an effort to obtain money to pay him.
they do not write an adrakhta, etc.. Even after the adrakhta stage has arrived, the borrower must be notified of it, unless he is far from the court.

and likewise if the document was for a deposit, they do not wait ninety days for him. Some explained that the reason is that only in a loan is he given time, because the lender took into account that he might not receive his money immediately, but in a deposit, which should be in the bailee's hand, the depositor expects to receive his deposit immediately (Maggid Mishneh, and see further explanations among the Rishonim on Bava Kamma 112b).
lest he consume them. For fear that he will use them up and lose the movables.
and even if the lender had land. And the borrower would be able to collect from it if the movables are used up.
lest it turn to ruin or be damaged. It will spoil, and he will have nothing to take.
they say. They write in the document.
they assess for him three of that field in the amount of his debt. Three people designate a plot of the field that, in their assessment, is worth the same as the debt.
and they announce it as they see fit. They announce publicly that this plot is up for sale at the price at which they assessed it.

until the bidders stop. In collecting free land there is no fixed length of time for the announcement; rather they announce until there are no more people willing to raise the price (compare below halakhah 9).
to the portion that they assessed. To the portion worth the debt according to their assessment.
and they tear up the promissory note. With the writing of the adrakhta (as below halakhah 13).
and they gave authority. This is the adrakhta.
and his hand extended. To collect and take possession.
from such-and-such time onward. From the time of the loan, when the lien took effect.
the shetar tirpa. A document of seizure.
and we have already torn up the adrakhta. With the writing of the shetar tirpa.
experts. In assessment.
from the principal and half of the improvement. They designate a plot such that the value of its principal plus half of what the buyer improved in it equals the debt.
as we have explained. Above 21:1.

and they announce it for thirty days. Unlike free property, where the length of the announcement is not fixed but depends on the judges' judgment according to the presence of buyers (as above, halakhah 6), with mortgaged property and orphans' property they are more exacting and the announcement period is a fixed thirty days (Maggid Mishneh).
in the way that they announce orphans' property. Thirty consecutive days, or sixty days on Mondays and Thursdays (see above 12:8).
they make the borrower swear that he has nothing, by enactment of the Geonim. The oath instituted by the Geonim mentioned above 2:2.
if the borrower was with us in the country. But if he is not in the country and cannot be made to swear, they do not delay the seizure for this.

and they make the seizer swear, etc.. For if the borrower claimed that he repaid and demanded that the lender swear, they would make him swear (above 14:2), and they argue on behalf of the buyer what the borrower could have argued (Rashi, Ketubot 87a).
and he did not sell it to another. For if the lender sold the debt to another, he has no right to collect it.
in his assessed portion. In the land assessed from it against the debt.
the horadah. The deed of descent, which is the final document of seizure from buyers.
and we made this seizer swear. The lender.
and the one who owes the debt. The borrower.
from when the announcement ended. From the moment the days of announcement are completed, even before the field reached his hand, the produce belongs to the lender.
it is not a hadrakhah. The adrakhta document is invalid.
and every assessment. The horadah document.
three who went down to assess, etc.. And they do not agree on the value of a certain piece of land.
the individual is nullified by the majority. And they follow the other two.
for a maneh. For one hundred.
he is judged at one hundred ten. For they rule according to the average between the two extreme amounts and not according to the average of all three.
and they erred. In the assessment.

and they erred by any amount, their sale is void, for they are like an agent, etc.. Because the court's action in this case is not by virtue of being a court but as agents of the seizer and of the buyer, their law is that of an agent who erred, and when an agent erred by any amount the sale is void (see Hilchot Mekhirah 13:9). However, when a court acts by virtue of being a court, such as in selling orphans' property, where their error was less than a sixth of the property's value, the sale stands (as above 12:11).
and all the teachers ruled thus. All the halakhic authorities ruled this way.
the one from whom it was seized. The buyer.
for the assessed land. Land that was collected by the court.
returns to the owners forever. Even after a long time.

and afterward the court assessed it to a creditor of this lender. After the court collected the land from the owners and brought it to the lender, they took it from him and brought it to his own creditor. ['Shamuha' is an alternate spelling of 'shamuh', and so it is in many versions, and the spelling here is a habit from Aramaic and Arabic - R. Y. Shilat.]
it returns. To the original owners, just as it returns from the first creditor.

his power should not be greater than the power of the first creditor. Since it too came to him through a court assessment, and he too is obligated to return it by the rule 'and you shall do what is right and good.'
the creditor sold it or gave it as a gift. The creditor who seized the land sold it or gave it as a gift to another person.
or he assessed it to his creditor with his consent. That the borrower himself handed over the field as repayment to his creditor and it was not given to him by the court.

it does not return. For in a sale or gift, receipt of the land is not receipt for the sake of the money in the land but receipt of the land itself, and therefore the land does not return to the original owners; and when the borrower handed over the field to the creditor of his own will, it is considered a sale (Bavli Bava Metzia 35a-b).
they assessed land for the woman. For a debt owed to her.
and she married. Afterward she married and her property entered her husband's possession.
or they assessed from her. In a case where she was the debtor.
and she married. Afterward.
a husband in his wife's property is like a buyer. The Sages gave the husband the status of a buyer with respect to his wife's property.
and does not return. When she collected through a court assessment before she married him, like the law of a lender who sold land that was assessed to him.

and they do not return to him. If they collected from his wife through a court assessment. He does not stand in his wife's place, since he is like a buyer of her property, and only to the borrower's heir do they return (as above halakhah 16), and not to one who bought his monetary rights.

post-dated promissory notes. Where the date written in the document is earlier than the time at which the debt's lien took effect. For example, the loan was on the first of Nisan and they wrote in the document the first of Adar.

for they seize buyers with them improperly. For on the basis of the document he can collect from property acquired after the date written in it, even though it was sold before the time of the loan and was never mortgaged to the debt.

and he collects with a pre-dated document only from free property. He may collect only from property in the borrower's hands, and not from property he sold or gave, even though it left his possession after the actual time of the loan and is mortgaged to the loan.

a decree, lest he seize with it from the earlier time to which he advanced it. They decreed to invalidate this document and not to collect mortgaged property on its basis, for fear that property would be collected with it according to the date written in it, which precedes the actual time of the loan.
post-dated documents of later date. Where the date in the document is later than the time at which the debt's lien took effect.

for the power of the document's holder is weakened, as he seizes only from the time of the document. Because of the later date the lender can only lose, in that he cannot collect from property that was mortgaged to the loan at its true time. For example, if the loan was on the first of Adar and the document says the first of Nisan, he cannot seize property that was sold to buyers from Adar until Nisan, even though it is mortgaged to the loan.
because it is early. For the document bears the date of writing, and the lien began only later when they signed the document at night.

even though they made the kinyan from him at night. Although ordinarily the lien takes effect from the time they performed the kinyan (see below halakhah 5), since they were engaged in the matter the whole time and were ready to sign, this has publicity as if they had already signed and the lien took effect from then.

on Shabbat or on the tenth of Tishrei. For certainly it was not written on Shabbat or on Yom Kippur, but on another day, and it is not clear whether it was written beforehand and a later date was written, or was written afterward and the date was advanced.
rather, they leave the document on its presumption. For a document's presumption is that it is valid until proven otherwise.
they write a document for the borrower. If he comes to witnesses and tells them to write a document in which they testify that he owes money to so-and-so.
in a document that has a kinyan in it. Where the document's witnesses perform a kinyan from him that he owes (see above 11:1).
for from the moment they made the kinyan from him his property was mortgaged. And it turns out that the time written in the document is the time the lien began.
but a document that has no kinyan in it. The lien begins only at the time the document is delivered to the lender.
and he will not borrow from him until Tishrei. And his property will be mortgaged only then, and it turns out the document is pre-dated.
witnesses who performed a kinyan from the borrower or the seller. And the lien or sale takes effect immediately and the document is written as evidence only.
they write in the document the time of the kinyan. For then the borrower's property became mortgaged.
even though it is not the time of their signing. The date written in the document is not the time of signing.
and they need not say, etc.. They need not state this in the document.
and if they did not know... they write the date of the document from the time of writing. And they do not write an estimated date of the time of the kinyan.
the place where they wrote their signature. They write in the document that it was written in such-and-such a place where they signed it.

for the seller returned and bought the field from the buyer before the time of the later document arrives. After he sold the field, the seller bought it back, at a time earlier than the date of the purchase that appears in the buyer's later document.

and the other will produce the later document. Since the date in the buyer's purchase document is later than the time at which the seller bought the field back, the buyer can claim that he bought the field from him again, since his purchase document bears a date later than the time at which the seller bought the field back.
lest he repay it before its time arrives. That the borrower repay the document before the loan date written in the loan document.
a receipt. A document of acknowledgment attesting that the debt was paid.
and he will again produce the later document and seize with it improperly. And the receipt will not help, since the date written on it precedes the loan time written in the document.
his remedy is to write the receipt without a date. There is a way to prevent double collection, by writing the receipt undated.
this receipt will break it. The receipt will serve as proof of repayment of the debt.
and he wrote the receipt at the time of repayment. He wrote on it the date of repayment.

and gave a modaah. He announced in advance to witnesses that the sale he is going to make is not with his consent, and he cancels it in advance. And therefore the coercer did not acquire (see Hilchot Mekhirah 10:1).
or he got ahead and sold or gave to another. And the coercer did not acquire.

and he does not seize anything with the bill of sale in his hand. If the seller cannot pay back to the coercer the money he gave him, the coercer cannot collect with the bill of sale from the seller's mortgaged property.
because the law of this document is not that it be written. And this is not like a sale by document.
but by oral testimony. And not by virtue of a debt by document.
that the judgment was concluded. Was ruled in court.
therefore, etc.. Since there are cases where they seize even without a document, concern arises about scheming and fraud.

and the buyer will return and seize with the bill of sale in his hand from the buyers who bought after him. The buyer will collect properly with the bill of sale from those who bought fields after him from the same seller, for the fields they bought are mortgaged to the earlier buyers.
and he will tear up the bill of sale in his hand. As part of the seizure procedure (compare above 22:13).

and he will return by collusion and remain in the field that was seized from him. After the buyer properly seized, with the bill of sale in his hand, from those who bought after him, the son will let him return and hold the land, and then the son will seize the field from the buyer by means of witnesses that the land belongs to his father, and the buyer will use the second bill of sale to collect fraudulently from further buyers who bought from the seller after the buyer.
one does not collect with this document, etc.. The document has no force for collection but is only testimony to the fact of the acquisition.

even though its witnesses are established and they made a kinyan from him. Even if they made a kinyan on the loan, in which case the witnesses of the kinyan can write a document on the debt (above 11:1).

and he returned at the time and said, 'The document you wrote for me now was lost or burned'. Even if he returned immediately after the writing ('at the time') and told the witnesses that the document they wrote for him just now was burned or lost.
they do not write him a second document. Even without responsibility.
lest he repaid it or forgave it. For it is possible that the borrower already repaid the debt or the lender forgave it to him.

and even if the debt was for a set time. Although there is a presumption that a person does not repay within the term, and here the lender comes immediately after the document was written, since now the lender has no document, the presumption is void and we suspect that the debt was repaid or forgiven (see above 14:13).

for this one is established as a liar by their testimony. If the borrower claims that he never borrowed, the witnesses of the loan contradict his words. And since the borrower is established as a liar, he is not believed afterward to claim that he paid the debt.
as will be explained. Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 6:1.
he stations witnesses over him. Who will testify about the content of the document in case it is erased before he manages to come to court (Maggid Mishneh).
and they make a qiyum for him. They write a document confirming the content that appeared in the worn document (as explained below halakhah 13).

but the witnesses of the document themselves do not write him another document, etc.. Even the same witnesses who signed the first document are forbidden to write a new document from what they remember, even though they know that the first document was erased. Rather, they come to court and give their testimony.

and if they wrote and we were required to rely on the testimony of the witnesses, etc.. If the court examined the signature of the witnesses ('the testimony of the witnesses') and found it reliable ('established'), the judges write a confirmation of the reliability of the worn document (see Hilchot Edut 6:2). And if they did not examine this, but confirm only the content that was in it, the testimony must be verified before collecting with it.
if its writing is recognizable. It is clear what is written in it.
it was torn with a court tear. A tear made by a court so that it not be collected with.
warp and woof. Lengthwise and widthwise (see also Hilchot Gerushin 4:16).
if he wishes, he exchanges, etc.. He brings the document in his hand to the court, and they write him a new document for the remaining amount, and write the date that was in the first document.
but not the witnesses of the document. The witnesses of the first document cannot on their own write him a document for the remaining debt.
a receipt. A document of acknowledgment to the borrower of what he paid, while the promissory note remains with the lender.
one who comes to repay all his debt. And the lender must give him the document or tear it up.

and the borrower may place a plain ban on one who withholds the document and claims it was lost. For the borrower loses by not receiving the document, since he must take care to keep his receipt. Therefore he may place a plain ban on one who hides the promissory note with him and claims that it was lost (see above 1:4 and the commentary there).
a maneh. One hundred dinars.
make two of it for me, fifty each. He asked that the debt be split into two documents, each for half the amount.

for if he repays part of it, his document turns out to be impaired. For if he repays part of the debt and after some time the lender claims the remainder, he will have to swear on his claim, since in any case where the amount written in the document is not identical to the amount of the claim, one collects only with an oath (above 14:1).

rather, they make a qiyum for each one separately, etc.. The documents are not merged, but the lender must authenticate each document separately, as it is more convenient for the borrower that each document be a separate claim.
we do not listen to him. Even though it would seem to be for the borrower's benefit.
and the borrower will produce the receipt. For a debt of one hundred.
we have already explained. Above 23:5.
and likewise they write a document for the seller. See Hilchot Mekhirah 30:1.
a receipt. A document of acknowledgment that the debt was paid.
and a receipt for the woman. On repayment of her ketubah.
and a get for the man even though his wife is not with him. See Hilchot Gerushin 2:3-4.
documents of betrothal. A document in which he betroths, or a document of conditions (see Lechem Mishneh, Ishut 3:4).
and marriage. A ketubah document in which the dowry the woman brought is also stated.
and documents of sharecropping and contracting. Various contractual agreements between the owner of a field and the one who works it in his place.
and documents of choosing the judges. When the litigants choose the judges themselves (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 7:1).
or documents of the claims of litigants. A detailing of the claims of both sides.
and every act of the court. Actions done by decision of the judges, which are written in a document (see Hilchot Yom Tov 7:12).
only with the knowledge of both of them. For all these documents obligate both parties.
must be careful in their drafting like other documents. As explained below chapter 27.
and who pays the scribe's fee?. Which party pays the scribe who writes the document.
and the woman pays the fee for the get. See also Hilchot Gerushin 2:4.
documents that are written for one not in the presence of his fellow. For example, a promissory note with a kinyan, which may be written without the lender being present.
and both of them are standing. Present at the writing.
collusion. Scheming and fraud.

and they will change their names to the names of others and admit to one another. They will use the identities of others and admit to each other a debt or sale or the like and write a forged document about it, and afterward use the document against one whose name is like that of the debtor written in the document.
for if you say so, there is no end to the matter. If we say that even after thirty days one cannot rely on the name by which a person has been established, then we cannot rely on names at all.
that I owe to so-and-so. A certain person who is not present before us.
or to this one. A person who is present before us.
he raised his name to be like my name. He changed his name for the purpose of the collusion and signed in my name.

since no two with the same names have been established there. It is not known that there is another person in the town whose name and father's name are identical to the name of the borrower or lender (such as two called Joseph son of Shimon, as below halakhah 8).
adults and of sound mind. For otherwise, a document is not written about them (see below 26:10-11).
and they cut paper for them and signed on the impression. They made cuts in the paper in the shape of the witnesses' names and filled them with ink.
the matter of the document. For what it was written.
his scribe. A permanent scribe.
since he trusts him and his fear is upon him. The head of the court relies on the scribe, and his fear is imposed on the scribe.
they cannot produce a promissory note on one another. For each of them can claim that the other is the one who borrowed from him.
nor can another produce a promissory note against them. For perhaps he lent to the other Joseph son of Shimon and not to the defendant.

unless the witnesses of the document come themselves and say, 'This is the one we testified about'. Another person can produce a promissory note against Joseph son of Shimon only if the document's witnesses testify which Joseph son of Shimon they testified received the loan (Perishah, Choshen Mishpat 49:12).

and this is the one for whom we testified about this loan. Joseph son of Shimon can produce a note against the other Joseph son of Shimon only if the document's witnesses testify that this is the Joseph son of Shimon for whom they testified that he gave a loan (ibid.).
and likewise they do not divorce their wives except in the presence of one another. For fear that they would give the get to the other man's wife (see Hilchot Gerushin 2:3).
and likewise if one finds among his documents a receipt, etc.. That he has a receipt that he paid the debt of Joseph son of Shimon.
the documents of both that are against him are paid. For when each of these two Josephs son of Shimon comes to claim from him, he will show him the receipt and say that his document is paid.
they should triple. They add to their name and their father's name the name of their father's father.
they should write their signs. In addition to their names they specify a sign by differing appearance and the like, for example 'Joseph son of Shimon the tall.'
they should write lineages. In a case where one is a kohen and the other an Israelite and the like.
they should write generations. They repeat the names of their forefathers for as many generations as needed until they are distinguished.
he produced against him a document, etc.. The lender produced against the borrower a document stating that the borrower owes him money, and the lender's name is not specified in it.
for this document came out from his possession. For the document was found with him.
this one for a hundred and this one for a hundred. If both debts were in the same amount and they come to collect from each other.
best, middling, poorest. Lands of different quality, the best being the finest of them.
if this one had best and middling, etc.. When the two do not have land of the same quality, each collects his debt separately according to the rules of collection, and the debts are not first offset.
this one collects from the middling. By the law of a lender who collects his debt from the middling (above 19:1).
and this one collects from the poorest. For when there is no middling, the law is that one is repaid from the poorest (ibid. halakhah 4).
if they were in a place where the buyer gives the money and afterward writes, etc.. And he could have taken the money and then retracted from the sale and kept the money as repayment of the debt.
so that you will have known assets. To prevent the borrower from evading repayment by concealing his ownership of the field.
and the other produces a document that he sold him the field. The borrower produces a document according to which the lender sold him land after the loan.
I am a guarantor. Responsible to repay the debt if the borrower does not repay it.
leave him alone and I am guarantor. Leave him now, and if he does not pay you after some time, I will guarantee for him.
he presses him. Pushes him.
the guarantor is not obligated to pay anything. Since a mere statement does not obligate.
but if they made a kinyan from him. If they performed a kinyan sudar with him to express the seriousness of his intent (see Hilchot Mekhirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
in all these ways. In all the cases mentioned.
at the time of giving the money. At the time of the loan.
the guarantor became obligated. In return for the benefit that the lender trusted and spent money on his word.
and likewise if the court made him a guarantor. Even after the loan.
he obligated himself for that benefit. In return for the benefit of being trusted.

but if the borrower has property, he does not collect from the guarantor at all. Even though the borrower refuses to repay the debt, he may not collect from the guarantor, but collects the debt from the borrower's property by order of the court (as explained above chapter 22).
an alam. A violent person.
to save from his hand. To collect from him or from his property.
they excommunicate. They ban him, since he does not accept the law upon himself (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:14).

on condition that I collect from whomever I wish, if the borrower has property he does not collect from the guarantor. For such a condition does not suffice to impose an additional lien on the guarantor; he is treated as an ordinary guarantor who is approached only when it becomes clear that the borrower cannot pay.
a kabbelan. See the next halakhah.

he may claim from this guarantor or from the kabbelan first. Since he explicitly stipulated that he would collect first from whomever he wishes, or because he is a kabbelan, whose responsibility for repaying the debt is greater (although if the lender claims from the borrower first, he cannot send him to the kabbelan - below 26:3).

this is a kabbelan from whom the lender may collect first. Since he spoke in the language of a gift, and did not mention at all the language of loan and repayment, it is understood that the kabbelan committed to give the money to the lender unconditionally, as if he himself had received it from the lender's hand.
all of them are the language of guaranty. And their meaning is that only if he does not succeed in collecting from the borrower will he collect from him.
unless he specifies and says, 'I will collect first from whomever I wish'. As above, halakhah 4.
a guarantor of a ketubah. One who guaranteed collection of a woman's ketubah money in case she is divorced or widowed.

even though they made a kinyan from him. Although in another debt, if they made a kinyan from the guarantor he is bound to the debt, even if he became a guarantor after the loan (as above, halakhah 1), in a ketubah the kinyan does not obligate him to pay.
for he performed a mitzvah. For he helped the couple marry.

and she lost no money. The woman does not lose money, since the ketubah does not come as repayment for money she spent. For these reasons the guarantor is not fully obligated (see also Hilchot Ishut 17:9).
and if the father was guarantor for his son's ketubah... he is obligated. Since it is his son, he resolves in his mind to obligate himself in this.
and a kabbelan of a ketubah. One who guaranteed the ketubah in the language of kabbelanut, for example by saying to her, 'Marry this man and I will give this ketubah'.
he is obligated. Even if it is not for his son's ketubah.

and he accepted responsibility for it upon himself. He accepted upon himself that if the field is taken from Shimon for any reason, for instance if it is shown that it was not Reuven's or if Reuven's creditors seize it to repay their debt, he will pay Shimon its value.

asmakhta. A commitment dependent on a future condition, which has no acquisitive force because the one transferring thinks the condition will not be fulfilled and does not firmly resolve to transfer (see Hilchot Mekhirah 11:2).

and if they made a kinyan from him that he is a guarantor to pay the price of this sale whenever Shimon demands it from him, he is obligated. When Levi's commitment was made as a guarantee of payment similar to a guarantee on a loan, he has the law of an ordinary guarantor, in which there is no problem of asmakhta (see Maggid Mishneh, Kesef Mishneh and others).
who obligated themselves on a condition. Who took the guarantee upon themselves on a future condition.
he is not bound because it is an asmakhta. Since he made his obligation depend on a future condition, he thinks the condition will not be fulfilled and did not firmly resolve to obligate himself.
two who borrowed by one document or took one purchase. Both borrowed or bought together, as partners.
in partnership. For the partnership.
they are guarantors for each other. So that if he cannot collect his share from one of them, he collects the whole debt from the other.
that he did not specify. They did not agree explicitly that they would be guarantors for each other.
and one who guaranteed two. A guarantor for two people who borrowed from one man.
he should inform him whose debt he is repaying. The lender should inform the guarantor whose debt of the two he is repaying.
so that he may return against him. So that the guarantor can claim the loan from that borrower, and the borrower cannot put him off by saying that he did not pay for him.
guarantee this one for so-and-so and I am guarantor to you. Take a guarantee on the debt of a certain person, and I will be a guarantor to you for this commitment.
one who did not specify the fixed amount of the thing for which he stood as guarantor. He took upon himself a general guarantee of his fellow's transactions, without defining a fixed sum.
or sell to him and I am guarantor. See above, halakhah 7.
and did not obligate himself. He did not firmly resolve to obligate himself (see also Hilchot Mekhirah 11:16 regarding a commitment to give an unspecified thing).
he did not guarantee the money itself, etc.. He did not take upon himself a guarantee for the loan, but that he would bring the borrower before him to court whenever the lender wishes.
and they made a kinyan from him on this. And thereby he became a guarantor even after the money was given (as above, halakhah 1).

there are Geonim who ruled that he must pay. In their view the meaning of a guarantee to bring him is that if he does not bring him he will pay, and therefore even if he did not guarantee the money itself, he must pay (see Maggid Mishneh).

for even if he stipulated with him and said, etc.. Even if he explicitly stated that he would pay if he did not bring him, he is not obligated to pay, since he did not firmly resolve to obligate himself in this.
and after the witnesses testified in the document. After the witnesses signed the document.
as we have explained. Above 25:1.
he does not seize from mortgaged property. Since his guarantee is not written in the document, and oral debts are not seized from mortgaged property (above 11:4).
if the guarantor was in the body of the document. If the guarantee is stated in the loan document between the loan and the signatures of the loan's witnesses.

if they wrote 'So-and-so is guarantor'... he does not collect from his mortgaged property. Because he is only mentioned in the document, but did not take upon himself full responsibility like a lender by document.
and so-and-so is guarantor. With the conjunctive vav.

and they made a kinyan from the guarantor. Since he became guarantor after the money was given, he is not obligated unless they made a kinyan from him on this, as above 25:1 (Maggid Mishneh, and see Lechem Mishneh).
he collects from the guarantor's mortgaged property. Since it is evident from the wording of the document that he took upon himself a full lien.
and did not find property for him. He did not find property in his possession from which to collect.
he cannot collect from the guarantor. To take land from him for repayment of the debt.

his power should not be less than the borrower himself. For if he asked to be allowed to obtain money so that land not be taken from him, they wait thirty days for him (see above 22:1, Maggid Mishneh).
and if he stipulated with him. If the lender agreed with the guarantor to collect in a different manner.
that he cannot inform him. That he is being sued.
nor go to him. To go to him and claim there.
for the court does not concern itself with their property. As explained above 12:1.
he claims from the guarantor first, for the borrower is not available. Provided that the borrower has no property there either (Kesef Mishneh).

he cannot put him off and say to him, 'Go to the kabbelan,' etc.. Although the kabbelan's responsibility is greater than that of an ordinary guarantor and the lender may collect from him first (above 25:4), the lender may collect from the borrower.

and if the kabbelan took the money, etc.. If he himself took the loan money from the lender and passed it to the borrower, it turns out that he is the borrower, and he is the only one obligated to repay the debt.
that the borrower swear by the enactment of the later authorities. The oath instituted by the Geonim for a borrower who claims he has nothing to pay with (above 2:2).

lest they collude regarding the guarantor's property. We suspect a fraudulent act, that the lender will claim that the borrower has no property and the borrower will admit to his words, and he will collect from the guarantor and they will divide the money between them.

the guarantor says to him, 'Bring proof,' etc.. For only in a loan by a document can the lender prove, from the very fact that the document is in his hand, that the debt was not repaid, whereas in an oral loan the lender must prove that his debt was not repaid.

even if it was an oral loan or without any witnesses. Although in these cases the borrower could have been exempt from paying the debt by claiming that he had paid it, since the borrower appointed him guarantor of this debt, he must pay him if he paid the debt.
when the borrower said... 'Guarantee me and pay'. Thereby he gave him full authority to repay his debt.
the borrower is not obligated to pay him anything. For the borrower did not authorize him to repay the debt on his own initiative, and it may be that the borrower would not have needed to pay at all.

and likewise one who repays the promissory note of his fellow, etc.. Even in a loan by a document or against a pledge, where the borrower cannot claim that he paid, he can nevertheless claim that he would have been exempt from payment by forgiveness, and therefore the borrower need not pay the one who paid for him.
that he admitted it. Close to his death (see above 11:6).

that they excommunicated him and he died under his ban. They banned the father because he did not wish to repay the debt, and he died before they lifted the ban; and had he paid, they would have lifted the ban from him.
or that the loan's time to be collected had not yet arrived. And there is a presumption that a person does not repay his debt within its term.

he returns and collects from the heirs everything he paid. In all these cases it is clear that the debt was not repaid, and since the guarantor was liable for the debt and had paid it first, the guarantor may collect what he paid from the heirs.
because the gentile claims the guarantor first. For this is accepted in gentile law, and we suspect that this is why the father took care before his death to pay the guarantor.
but if he informed them that the gentile is claiming from him, etc.. For it is evident from his words that he did not pay the guarantor in advance.
and the finding of the promissory note in the guarantor's hand is not proof. He cannot present the promissory note as proof that he paid the debt and that is why the lender gave it to him.
lest the document fell from the lender's hand. And the guarantor found it.
one who says to his fellow, 'You guaranteed for me'. And since I cannot repay, you must repay in my place.
or the guarantor said to the borrower, 'You authorized me to guarantee you and to give'. And he demands that he pay him what he paid.
'You guaranteed with your knowledge' or 'You did not guarantee at all'. In these cases the borrower is not obligated to pay the one who paid for him (as above, halakhah 6).
like other monetary claims. See Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:1-3.
a slave or a married woman. Who have no property of their own (for a similar law see Hilchot Chovel 4:21).
even though they made a kinyan from him. Ordinarily, if a kinyan was made from the borrower, this can be written in the document (above 11:1).
for a kinyan from a minor is nothing. Commitments made by kinyan sudar do not take effect for a minor (see Hilchot Mekhirah 29:9).
she is obligated to pay after she marries. Even though her property is under her husband's control.

for a husband's domain is like a buyer's domain. The Sages gave the husband the status of a buyer with respect to his wife's property, and therefore debts written in a document can be collected from it as from mortgaged property, but not oral debts.
as we have explained in several places. Above 22:17, Hilchot Zekhiyah u-Matanah 12:12, Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 2:11.
and if the loan money itself still exists, they return it to the lender. Even in an oral loan.
in any language and in any script. In any language and any form of writing.
in the manner of the documents of Israel. As detailed later in the chapter.
that cannot be forged, nor added to, nor subtracted from. They are written in such a way that any forgery, addition or erasure is visible to the eye.
and they know how to read it. Witnesses do not sign a document unless they can read it (above 24:5).
whose signers. The witnesses who signed them.
except for documents of sale and promissory notes. Which serve as evidence only.
in their courts. In the gentile courts.

but in a place where their criminal courts convene, without the confirmation of their judge. If it was done in a place where they gathered to judge, without one of their judges attesting in his own handwriting that the witnesses' testimony was found reliable.
documents of admission. A document in which a person admits a debt.
and gifts. A document in which one transfers land to his fellow.
and compromises. A document in which the litigants accept a certain compromise upon themselves.
and waivers. A document in which a person waives a monetary matter or monetary right against his fellow.
they are like a potsherd. For in all of these the acquisition and obligation depend on the document itself.
and I do not agree to this. Rather, the law of a promissory note is that of a bill of sale.
in courts. In the gentile courts.
like one who speaks innocently. Casual speech without intent to testify, in which case we believe them in certain testimonies (see Hilchot Gerushin 12:17, 13:29).
but one does not seize with it. One cannot collect from mortgaged property with documents signed by gentiles.
because it has no publicity. There is no publicity for such a document, and the buyer cannot guard against buying the borrower's mortgaged lands (compare above 11:4).

for the buyers did not know what was done among gentiles. For the signing witnesses are those who publicize the matter, by telling others what they signed. But with a document whose witnesses are gentiles the word does not get out among the Israelite buyers.

a document whose witnesses are gentiles, which was delivered... he collects with it from free property. For we rely on the witnesses of delivery for this (see above 11:2; and although it says there that one collects even from mortgaged property on the basis of a document delivered before witnesses, here, where the signing witnesses are gentiles, its force is weaker - Sema 68:18).
and why should he not collect with it from mortgaged property?. As with any promissory note.
because it has no publicity. As explained above, halakhah 1.
he must repeat something of the matter of the document in the last line. He should not add anything new in the last line, but repeat again something already written before it.
for one does not learn from the last line. The Sages enacted that what is written in the last line is not valid, and if he writes something new in it, it will be meaningless.

lest the witnesses be a line's distance from the body of the document. Witnesses are generally not trained in precise writing, and it is hard for them to sign right next to the end of the document, and sometimes an empty line remains before their signatures, and in that line the lender who holds the document could add a forgery.
witnesses who were two lines distant from the writing, it is invalid. Since one could add something in the line before the last that affects the content of the document.
the two lines that they said. When the Sages said that a distance of two lines invalidates the document.

by the handwriting of witnesses and not by the handwriting of a scribe, etc.. The width of a line is measured by the writing of a person not trained in writing, and not by the writing of a scribe who knows how to write in a measured way that takes less space, because the forger takes care not to forge in the style of an expert scribe.

and these two lines and their two spaces, such as a lamed over a kaf. The width of the two lines is not just the width of a letter above a letter, but one must add to each line the space above and below it for letters that extend upward or downward.
filled with invalid witnesses or relatives. Who signed there.
it is valid, for it cannot be forged. Since nothing additional can be written in the space (and invalid witnesses do not invalidate the document - see Hilchot Edut 5:6-7).
lest the witnesses signed on the scratches. It is possible that their signature refers to meaningless scratches and not to the document.
the entire document with its witnesses was on one line. The whole document is written on one line and the witnesses signed on the same line.

lest these witnesses were a line's distance from the valid document, etc.. We suspect that there were witnesses signed on a valid document at a distance of one line from the document, and the forger cut the valid document and left from it the signatures together with the empty line and wrote the forged document in it.

we do not authenticate this document from the lower witnesses, etc.. The court does not authenticate the document on the basis of the lower signatures, for fear that these signatures belong to another document and there was an empty line between it and the signatures, and the forger cut the document and in the empty line wrote the forged document and the witnesses' signatures.
the court's confirmation. The judges' approval of the validity of the document (see Hilchot Edut chapter 6).
adjacent to the handwriting of the witnesses. Beneath the signatures.
and we are not concerned about a court, etc.. Witnesses may sign on something trivial (above, halakhah 4), but a court does not sit to sign on such a thing.

all erasures, one must write their confirmation, etc.. If there are changes in the document made after the writing, such as a word that was erased and another written in its place, or a word added between the lines ('hanging'), one must confirm the changes at the end of the document before the witnesses' signatures. The confirmation is done by specifying the changes and then writing 'and everything is firm and established.' Otherwise there is concern that the erasure was made after the witnesses signed the document and changed its meaning (see also Hilchot Gerushin 4:15).

and if the erasure was in the place of 'firm and established' and the size of 'firm and established'. If there is an erasure at the end of the document in the place where 'and everything is firm and established' is customarily written, and the erasure extends over a space in which 'firm and established' could be written.

lest he erased it and wrote something he forged, and then confirmed it in the space between the writing and the witnesses. Perhaps the lender erased the words 'and everything is firm and established' that mark the end of the document, and in their place wrote something in his favor, and afterward confirmed the erasure he made in the empty line before the witnesses' signatures.

a document in which it and its witnesses are on an erasure. The content of the document and the witnesses' signatures were written over an erasure (on parchment one can erase writing by scraping off the ink and then write again, and when there is writing over an erasure this is visible to the eye).

one that was erased once is not like one erased twice. There is no need to fear that after the writing he will erase the content of the document and write what he wants, for then the witnesses' signatures would be over one erasure and the document's content over two erasures, and the difference is visible to the eye.

and if you say, perhaps he erased the place of the witnesses twice. One might apparently worry that he had erased the place of the document once beforehand and the place of the signatures twice, and could now erase the document a second time, so that its erasure would match the signed area and he could write another document.

the Sages already enacted that witnesses not sign on an erased document, etc.. The Sages enacted that witnesses not sign a document written on erased parchment unless they saw the erasure, and so they will not sign a document whose erasure is not uniform.
and the confirmation is below on the paper. The judges' attestation to the validity of the testimony was in the lower area that was not erased.
we do not authenticate it from the witnesses of the confirmation. One cannot validate the document on the basis of the judges' signatures in the confirmation.
and the space was full of ink scratches. And they wrote the confirmation under the scratches (as above, halakhah 7).
and he cut the body of the document. He cut the upper document together with the witnesses' signatures on it so that he could collect with it.

and erased the scratches and wrote a document and its witnesses on the erasure. He wrote another document with forged signatures over the scratches he erased, and now it appears that the confirmation refers to the forged document.

a document that is on paper and its witnesses on an erasure. The document itself is written on ordinary parchment from which nothing was erased, and the witnesses signed below in a place that had been erased.
and they write it so between witness and witness so that he not forge. For if they write it elsewhere, it could be erased as part of erasing the document.
for if there were room... it would be noticeable. But when part is erased and part is not erased, it is not apparent how many times the erased part was erased.

and from the correction of documents, etc.. The correction of documents (above, halakhah 3) also includes the care of the judge who looks at the form of the writing and checks that a thin letter such as vav or zayin was not added between words.
and they should not be distant. That there is no unnecessary space between the letter vav and the word that follows it.
and he left one leg in the place of a vav. He left only the right leg of the letter heh or chet, which looks like a vav.
from three to ten, they do not write at the end of a line. If he comes to write in letters a number from three to ten, he should not write it at the end of a line.
lest he forge, etc.. He will add a little at the edge of the line.
and he shall return. He shall turn.

he repeats the statement, etc.. He repeats and states as many times as needed that he obligated himself for this sum, until it happens that he writes the sum in the middle of a line, and the last mention is what determines (as explained in the next halakhah).
everything goes after the lower. For it is to be assumed that in the middle of writing it was decided to change the amount of the loan.
because one does not depend on the other. One amount is not an explanation or detail of the other amount, but each stands on its own.

for if it were written in it 'a hundred which is two hundred' or 'two hundred which is a maneh,' he would take a hundred. Since it is uncertain what is meant, he is owed only a hundred, for the document holder's hand is at the bottom (see Hilchot Mekhirah 21:19).
if there was a name above, etc.. If there is a slight variation in the mentions of one of the names, we follow the lower.
if so, why do they write the upper, etc.. The benefit of writing the name twice is for the case where part of the lower name is erased, and one can learn the name from the upper mention.
and in the lower, Chanan or Anan. Where the letter yod was erased and it reads 'Chanan' or 'Anan'.

but he may not learn the lower from the upper by two letters. If above it is written 'Chanani' and below two letters were erased and it reads 'Chan', the document is invalid, for one letter may be erased by itself, but with two letters erased we must assume a deliberate erasure; and since the reason for the erasure is unknown, one cannot collect with this document.
sefel. An abbreviation of 'se'ah u-felaga', a se'ah and a half (Ri Migash and other Rishonim on Bava Batra 166b).
kefel. An abbreviation of 'kav u-felaga',

a kav and a half. And likewise anything similar to this, etc.. Although the rule is that we follow the lower one, if the difference can be explained by circumstance and not by a deliberate change in the writing, we are concerned about it and in every case follow the lesser amount, since the reason for the variation is uncertain and the document holder's hand is at the bottom.
an istera. Half a zuz.
a perutah. Which is a smaller coin.

the scribe totals them as zuzim and then writes them. It is not the scribe's way to state a large sum of perutot; rather he calculates how many zuzim these perutot are worth and states them by their value in zuzim.

a document in which is written 'istera, a hundred ma'ei' or in which is written 'a hundred ma'ei istera'. And there is doubt whether the word 'hundred' refers to the word 'ma'ei' (coins), so that he must pay him a sum of a hundred coins in istera coins, or whether the word 'hundred' refers to 'istera' and he must pay him a sum of a hundred isteras (which is much lower) in ma'ei coins (Yad Peshutah, and see Maggid Mishneh, who explained differently and emended the wording of Rambam, in line with Raavad's criticism).

and if he seized the upper, etc.. If the plaintiff seized from the defendant's property according to the higher sum, it is not taken out of his hand, since he is now the one in possession of the money and it is doubtful whether it should be taken from him.

no less than a gold dinar. For it is uncertain which coin is meant, and therefore he collects a dinar, which is the smallest coin commonly made of gold (for the smallest coins are made of silver or copper).
gold dinars or dinars of gold. And the number of coins is not specified.
no less than two gold dinars. The lender collects two dinars, since the minimum of the plural is two.
gold in dinars. Gold worth dinars, and there is doubt whether it means the value of silver dinars or the value of gold dinars.
no less than the value of two silver dinars in gold. The lender collects pieces of gold worth two silver dinars, since his hand is at the bottom.
